title: Green Lasagne alla Bolognese
instructions:
Green Lasagne alla Bolognese

Classic Bolognese lasagne with spinach-green pasta sheets, ragù, béchamel, and Parmigiano Reggiano.

Yield: 8 servings

Ingredients

For the green pasta
6 cups type 00 flour
3 fresh eggs
2 cups boiled spinach, squeezed very dry and chopped

For the béchamel
7 tbsp unsalted butter
3/4 cup plus 2 tbsp type 00 flour
4 1/4 cups whole milk
2 tsp fine salt
3/4 tsp freshly grated nutmeg

For the layers
4 cups plus 1 tbsp plus 1 tsp classic Bolognese ragù
4 cups freshly grated Parmigiano Reggiano
7 tbsp unsalted butter

For cooking the pasta
10.6 qt water
1/4 cup plus 1/4 tsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Make the green pasta. Mound the 6 cups flour on the work surface, form a well, and add the eggs and 2 cups chopped spinach. Knead until the dough is smooth, even, and elastic. Cover and rest for 1 hour.

2. Make the béchamel. Melt 7 tablespoons butter in a saucepan over low heat. Add the 3/4 cup plus 2 tablespoons flour and whisk until a uniform roux forms. Cook for 2 minutes without allowing it to darken.

3. Heat the 4 1/4 cups milk until steaming but not boiling. Add it to the roux in several additions, whisking continuously. Add 2 teaspoons fine salt and 3/4 teaspoon nutmeg. Cook over low heat for 15 minutes, stirring continuously, until creamy and fluid.

4. Roll the pasta thin and cut it into 6 x 4-inch rectangles.

5. Pour 10.6 quarts water into a large stockpot, add 1/4 cup plus 1/4 teaspoon fine salt, and bring to a vigorous boil.

6. Cook the pasta sheets two at a time. Remove each sheet as soon as it rises to the surface, transfer immediately to cold water, and lay flat on a clean cotton or linen cloth until the surface is dry.

7. Preheat the oven to 350°F.

8. Grease a 10 x 14-inch rectangular baking dish at least 2 3/8 inches deep with 2 teaspoons of the butter reserved for assembly.

9. Divide the ragù and béchamel separately into 7 equal portions. Divide the 4 cups Parmigiano into 6 portions of 2/3 cup each.

10. Spread 1 portion of ragù and 1 portion of béchamel over the bottom of the dish.

11. Cover with the first pasta layer. Add 1 portion béchamel, 1 portion ragù, 1 tablespoon butter in small pieces, and 2/3 cup Parmigiano.

12. Repeat the same order until there are 6 pasta layers total. On each of the first 5 pasta layers, use 1 portion béchamel, 1 portion ragù, 1 tablespoon butter, and 2/3 cup Parmigiano.

13. On the sixth and final pasta layer, mix the last portion of ragù with the last portion of béchamel and spread it over the surface. Add the final 1 tablespoon butter, placing part of it in each corner, and finish with the final 2/3 cup Parmigiano.

14. Check that the layers are even and free of air pockets. Pierce the pasta in 3–4 places with a toothpick wherever trapped air remains.

15. Bake at 350°F for 25–30 minutes.

16. Rest for 5 minutes before cutting.

Serving

Cut into 8 portions and serve hot.

Chef's Note

Keep the béchamel fluid and creamy rather than thick. Even layers and balanced distribution of ragù, béchamel, butter, and Parmigiano prevent the lasagne from becoming unevenly dry or heavy.
history: Bologna’s green lasagne developed from Emilia-Romagna’s layered pasta tradition. The modern version pairs spinach pasta with ragù, béchamel, and Parmigiano Reggiano. In 2003, the Accademia Italiana della Cucina formally certified the recipe, which was registered with the Bologna Chamber of Commerce.
description: Silky spinach lasagne sheets cradle slow-cooked ragù, creamy béchamel, butter, and Parmigiano in rich, savory layers. title: Neapolitan Lasagna
instructions:
Neapolitan Lasagna

Rich Neapolitan lasagna with egg pasta sheets, slow-cooked meat sauce, tiny meatballs, ricotta, fiordilatte, hard-boiled eggs, and Parmigiano Reggiano.

Yield: 8 servings

Ingredients

For the pasta sheets
1 2/3 cups type 00 flour
1 1/4 cups fine durum-wheat semolina
4 large eggs

For the veal rolls and meat sauce
1 1/8 lb thin veal cutlets
1/4 cup finely grated Parmigiano Reggiano
1/4 cup finely chopped fresh parsley
6 fresh mint leaves, finely chopped
1 garlic clove, finely minced
2/3 lb fresh pork pancetta, cut into pieces
6 1/3 cups tomato passata
3/4 cup dry white or red wine
1 medium onion, diced
1 medium carrot, diced
1 celery stalk, diced
1/3 cup plus 1 tbsp plus 1 tsp extra-virgin olive oil
1 2/3 cups water
2 tsp fine salt

For the meatballs
1 1/8 lb ground veal or a veal-and-pork mixture
1 large egg
1/3 cup plus 1 tbsp finely grated Parmigiano Reggiano
1/4 cup finely chopped fresh parsley
3/4 tsp fine salt
4 1/4 cups peanut oil for frying

For assembly
4 hard-boiled eggs
1 1/8 lb well-drained fiordilatte or scamorza
2 cups ricotta
1 cup finely grated Parmigiano Reggiano

For cooking the pasta
6 1/3 qt water
2 tbsp plus 1 tsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Make the veal rolls. Divide the 1/4 cup Parmigiano, 1/4 cup parsley, mint, and garlic among the veal cutlets. Roll each cutlet tightly and secure it with kitchen twine.

2. Make the meat sauce. Heat the olive oil in a large heavy pot over medium heat. Add the onion, carrot, and celery and cook for 8 minutes, stirring, until softened without browning.

3. Add the veal rolls and pancetta. Brown for 10 minutes, turning the meat so all sides color evenly.

4. Pour in the 3/4 cup wine and cook for 3 minutes, until the sharp alcohol aroma has largely cooked away.

5. Add the 6 1/3 cups passata, 1 2/3 cups water, and 2 teaspoons salt. Bring to a gentle boil, then reduce the heat. Cook uncovered for 60 minutes over medium-low heat.

6. Reduce the heat to low and continue cooking for another 3 hours, stirring every 20–30 minutes. After about 2 hours of total cooking time, remove the veal rolls and pancetta and reserve them. Continue cooking the sauce until concentrated but still fluid.

7. Make the pasta dough. Combine the type 00 flour and semolina, form a well, and add the 4 eggs. Knead for 10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Cover and rest for 60 minutes.

8. Roll the dough through a pasta machine to setting No. 5, or to about 1/16 inch thick. Cut sheets to fit a roughly 13 x 9-inch baking dish. Lay them on clean towels and dry for 2 hours.

9. Make the meatballs. Combine the ground meat, egg, 1/3 cup plus 1 tablespoon Parmigiano, 1/4 cup parsley, and 3/4 teaspoon salt. Form small meatballs about 3/4 inch in diameter.

10. Heat the peanut oil to 350°F. Fry the meatballs in batches for 2–3 minutes, until lightly golden rather than deeply browned. Drain on paper towels.

11. Bring the 6 1/3 quarts water and 2 tablespoons plus 1 teaspoon salt to a boil. Cook the pasta sheets a few at a time for 1–2 minutes. Drain and lay flat on dry kitchen towels.

12. Slice the 4 hard-boiled eggs. Cut the fiordilatte or scamorza into 3/8-inch cubes. Stir 2/3 cup of the meat sauce into the 2 cups ricotta until creamy.

13. Preheat the oven to 350°F.

14. Spread 1 cup meat sauce over the bottom of the baking dish. Cover with one layer of pasta sheets.

15. Distribute portions of meat sauce, ricotta, fiordilatte, hard-boiled egg, meatballs, and Parmigiano over the pasta. Repeat in the same order until there are 5 pasta layers total, dividing the fillings evenly among the layers.

16. Finish the top layer with meat sauce and Parmigiano.

17. Bake at 350°F for 55–60 minutes, until heated through and lightly browned on top.

18. Rest for 20 minutes before cutting.

Service

Cut into 8 portions and serve hot, spooning a small amount of meat sauce over each portion.

Chef's note

Keep the meat sauce fluid enough to hydrate the pasta layers as the lasagna bakes. Drain the fiordilatte thoroughly before assembly so it does not release excess water into the dish.
history: A rich specialty of Naples, this lasagna is closely tied to Carnival, especially Shrove Tuesday, when extravagant meat-and-cheese dishes traditionally preceded Lent. Unlike the Bolognese version, it is built with ragù, ricotta, mozzarella, tiny meatballs, and often eggs or salami.
description: An extravagant baked centerpiece layered with slow-cooked ragù, creamy ricotta, melting cheese, tender lasagna, miniature meatballs, and hard-boiled eggs. Every slice is deeply savory, luxurious, and festive—the kind of dish designed for a long family meal.

title: Vincisgrassi
instructions:
Vincisgrassi

Marche-style layered pasta with Marsala-enriched sheets, meat and chicken-giblet ragù, béchamel, and Grana Padano.

Yield: 6 servings

Ingredients

For the pasta sheets
2 3/4 cups plus 1 tbsp type 00 flour
1 1/4 cups fine durum-wheat semolina
4 eggs
2 tbsp dry Marsala or vino cotto
1 1/2 tbsp softened butter
3/4 tsp fine salt

For the ragù
1 1/8 lb mixed veal and pork, knife-chopped or coarsely ground
2/3 lb cleaned chicken giblets, cut into pieces
1 tbsp minced lard
2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
1 onion
1 celery stalk
1 carrot
3 whole cloves
1 bouquet garni made with 1 bay leaf, 2 parsley sprigs, and 1 thyme sprig
3/4 cup plus 1 tbsp plus 1 tsp dry white wine
3/4 cup plus 1 tbsp plus 1 tsp whole milk
2 tbsp tomato paste
3/4 cup plus 1 tbsp plus 1 tsp tomato passata
2 cups plus 1 tbsp plus 2 tsp hot water
1 tsp fine salt
1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper

For the béchamel
3 tbsp butter
1/3 cup type 00 flour
2 cups plus 1 tbsp plus 2 tsp whole milk
2/3 tsp fine salt
1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper
1/4 tsp freshly grated nutmeg

For assembly
1 1/2 tbsp butter
3/4 cup finely grated Grana Padano

For cooking the pasta
5 1/4 qt water
2 tbsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Make the pasta dough. Combine the type 00 flour and semolina on the work surface. Form a well and add the 4 eggs, Marsala, softened butter, and salt.

2. Knead vigorously for 10 minutes until smooth and firm. Form into a ball, wrap, and rest for 30 minutes.

3. Roll the dough between 1/16 and 3/16 inch thick and cut it into rectangles sized for the baking dish.

4. Make the ragù. Stud the onion with the 3 cloves. Cut the onion, celery, and carrot into 2–3 large pieces so they can be removed at the end of cooking.

5. Heat the lard and olive oil in a wide pot. Add the vegetables, mixed meat, and chicken giblets. Brown over medium-high heat for 10 minutes.

6. Add 1 teaspoon salt and 1/2 teaspoon pepper. Pour in the white wine and cook for 3 minutes.

7. Add the warm milk. Cover and cook over medium-low heat for 30 minutes.

8. Add the tomato paste, passata, and bouquet garni. Pour in the hot water, stir, and bring to a gentle simmer.

9. Cook uncovered over low heat until the ragù has reduced by about one-third, 60–75 minutes. Remove the onion, celery, carrot, and bouquet garni. The sauce should remain soft and fairly fluid.

10. Make the béchamel. Melt the butter in a saucepan over low heat. Add the flour and whisk for 2 minutes.

11. Heat the milk, then whisk it gradually into the roux. Add the salt, pepper, and nutmeg. Cook over low heat for 10 minutes, stirring, until creamy but still pourable.

12. Bring the water and salt to a boil. Blanch the pasta rectangles a few at a time for 2–3 minutes. Remove with a slotted spoon and lay flat on a clean kitchen towel.

13. Grease a rectangular baking dish with the butter reserved for assembly.

14. Spread a thin layer of ragù over the bottom. Cover with pasta, then add béchamel, ragù, and part of the Grana.

15. Repeat in the same order until there are 8 pasta layers, distributing the ragù, béchamel, and cheese evenly.

16. Finish with a small amount of béchamel, ragù, and a more generous portion of the remaining Grana.

17. Cover and refrigerate the assembled dish for 2 hours.

18. Preheat the oven to 350°F. Bake for 40 minutes.

19. Rest at room temperature for 10 minutes before cutting.

Service

Cut into 6 portions and serve hot.

Chef's note

The ragù should remain soft and slightly fluid. If it is reduced too far, it will not hydrate all eight pasta layers properly during baking.
history: This festive baked pasta is a hallmark of the Marche. Its precise origins are debated. One long-standing tradition links its name to Austrian general Windisch-Graetz after the 1799 defense of Ancona, while culinary historians emphasize centuries of regional evolution and adaptation.
description: Thin pasta sheets alternate with an intensely savory ragù of meats and chicken offal, creamy béchamel, and aged cheese. The result is deeply layered, aromatic, rustic yet refined, and built for the grandest holiday table.

title: Pasta alla Norma
instructions:
Pasta alla Norma

Classic Catania pasta with tomato sauce, fried eggplant, ricotta salata, and basil.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

4 cups dry penne or macaroni
2 cups plus 1 tbsp plus 2 tsp tomato sauce
2 medium eggplants
3/4 cup finely grated ricotta salata
1 1/2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
1 garlic clove
1 cup loosely packed fresh basil leaves
4 1/4 cups peanut or sunflower oil for frying
1 2/3 tsp fine salt for the eggplant
1/3 tsp fine salt for the sauce

For cooking the pasta
4 1/4 qt water
1 tbsp plus 1 2/3 tsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Cut the eggplants into slices about 3/8 inch thick.

2. Layer the slices in a colander and distribute the 1 2/3 teaspoons salt evenly over them. Drain for 30 minutes.

3. Rinse the eggplant briefly and dry it completely with paper towels.

4. Heat the frying oil to 350°F. Fry the eggplant in batches for 2–3 minutes per side, until golden with a soft center. Drain on paper towels.

5. Heat the 1 1/2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil in a saucepan over medium-low heat. Add the garlic and cook for 2 minutes without browning it.

6. Add the tomato sauce, three-quarters of the basil, and 1/3 teaspoon salt. Cook over medium-low heat for 15 minutes.

7. Remove the garlic. Cut half of the fried eggplant into strips and stir it into the tomato sauce. Reserve the remaining slices for serving.

8. Bring the water and salt to a boil.

9. Cook the pasta until al dente and drain it.

10. Transfer the pasta to the tomato-and-eggplant sauce and toss over medium heat for 1 minute.

11. Finely grate the ricotta salata.

Service

Divide the pasta among 4 plates. Top with the reserved eggplant slices, ricotta salata, and remaining basil.

Chef's note

Dry the eggplant thoroughly before frying. Oil held at 350°F browns the slices quickly and limits excess oil absorption.
history: Originating in Catania, this Sicilian classic combines pasta, tomato, fried eggplant, basil, and ricotta salata. Tradition links its name to Vincenzo Bellini’s opera Norma, with one popular story crediting Catanese playwright Nino Martoglio for comparing the dish to the celebrated opera.

title: Pasta with Sardines
instructions:
Pasta with Sardines

Palermo-style bucatini with fresh sardines, wild fennel, anchovies, currants, pine nuts, saffron, tomato paste, and toasted breadcrumbs.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

7/8 lb bucatini
7/8 lb fresh sardines
6 packed cups wild fennel fronds
1 tbsp tomato paste
4 oil-packed anchovy fillets
1/4 cup dried currants
1/4 cup pine nuts
1 packet saffron
1/2 onion, finely chopped
3 tbsp plus 2 tsp extra-virgin olive oil for the sauce
1/4 cup dry breadcrumbs
2 1/4 tsp extra-virgin olive oil for the breadcrumbs
1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper
1/4 cup plus 2 tsp reserved fennel cooking water for the sauce
1 cup plus 1 tbsp hot water for soaking the currants

For cooking the fennel and pasta
4 1/4 qt water
1 tbsp plus 1 1/2 tsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Soak the currants in the hot water for 60 minutes, then drain.

2. Trim away the tough parts of the wild fennel and wash it thoroughly.

3. Bring the water and salt to a boil. Cook the fennel for 15 minutes.

4. Drain the fennel, chop it coarsely, and reserve all of its cooking water. Measure out 1/4 cup plus 2 teaspoons for the sauce.

5. Clean the sardines, removing the heads, innards, and center bones. Open them flat, rinse briefly, and dry thoroughly.

6. Finely chop the onion.

7. Heat the 3 tablespoons plus 2 teaspoons olive oil in a wide saucepan. Add the onion and anchovy fillets. Cook for 6 minutes, stirring until the anchovies dissolve.

8. Add the pine nuts, drained currants, and tomato paste. Cook for 2 minutes.

9. Add the sardines and cook over high heat for 3 minutes.

10. Add the chopped fennel.

11. Take 1 tablespoon of the measured fennel water and dissolve the saffron in it. Add the saffron mixture and the remaining fennel water to the pan.

12. Add the black pepper. Cover and cook over medium-low heat for 10 minutes.

13. Heat the 2 1/4 teaspoons olive oil in a skillet. Add the breadcrumbs and toast for 4–5 minutes, stirring, until golden and crisp.

14. Return the fennel cooking water to a boil and cook the bucatini in it.

15. Drain the bucatini while very al dente and transfer it to the saucepan with the sardine sauce.

16. Toss over medium heat for 2 minutes, distributing the sardines and fennel evenly.

Service

Divide among 4 plates and sprinkle the toasted breadcrumbs over the top.

Chef's note

Reusing the fennel cooking water for both the pasta and the sauce concentrates the herb's flavor. The anchovies also add salinity, so the measured salt is kept in the cooking water rather than added separately to the sauce.
history: Closely associated with Palermo, this Sicilian pasta unites sardines with wild fennel, saffron, raisins, pine nuts, anchovies, and breadcrumbs. Its origins are often linked by tradition to Sicily’s Arab period, reflecting the island’s historic blending of Mediterranean, North African, and local flavors. Its legacy endures.

title: Pasta ’Ncasciata
instructions:
Pasta ’Ncasciata

Messina-style baked pasta with meat ragù, fried eggplant, caciocavallo, salami, and hard-boiled eggs.

Yield: 6 servings

Ingredients

1 1/8 lb maccheroncelli
6 medium ripe sauce tomatoes
2 hard-boiled eggs
7/16 lb ground meat
3/4 cup diced salami
2 medium eggplants
1 1/2 cups caciocavallo, divided
2 garlic cloves
10 fresh basil leaves
1/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil
3 1/4 cups extra-virgin olive oil or peanut oil for frying
1 tbsp plus 1/3 tsp fine salt for the eggplant
3/4 tsp fine salt for the sauce
1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper
1/3 cup dry breadcrumbs
1/2 cup hot water

For cooking the pasta
5 1/4 qt water
2 tbsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Peel the eggplants and cut them into slices about 3/8 inch thick.

2. Layer the slices in a colander, distribute the 1 tablespoon plus 1/3 teaspoon salt evenly over them, and rest for 60 minutes.

3. Rinse the eggplant briefly to remove surface salt and dry it completely.

4. Heat the frying oil to 350°F. Fry the eggplant in batches until golden, about 2–3 minutes per side. Drain on paper towels.

5. Heat 3 tablespoons of the extra-virgin olive oil in a saucepan. Add the whole garlic cloves and cook for 2 minutes. Remove the garlic when golden.

6. Add the ground meat and brown for 5 minutes, breaking it apart with a spoon.

7. Peel and chop the tomatoes. Add them to the meat with the basil, 3/4 teaspoon salt, and 1/2 teaspoon pepper.

8. Pour in the 1/2 cup hot water. Cook over low heat for 50 minutes, stirring every 10 minutes, until the sauce is thick but still fluid enough to coat the pasta.

9. Slice the hard-boiled eggs. Dice the salami. Dice 1 1/4 cups of the caciocavallo and finely grate the remaining 1/4 cup.

10. Bring the water and salt to a boil. Cook the maccheroncelli until 3 minutes short of the package's stated cooking time. Drain.

11. Toss the pasta with all of the ragù.

12. Preheat the oven to 350°F.

13. Grease a baking dish with the remaining 1 tablespoon olive oil and coat the bottom evenly with the breadcrumbs.

14. Spread one-third of the sauced pasta in the dish. Add one-third of the fried eggplant, diced caciocavallo, hard-boiled egg, and salami.

15. Repeat for two more layers, finishing with pasta. Scatter the reserved grated caciocavallo over the surface.

16. Bake at 350°F for 30 minutes, until the cheese is melted and the top is lightly browned.

17. Rest for 10 minutes before cutting.

Service

Divide into 6 portions and serve hot.

Chef's note

Drain the pasta very al dente because it finishes cooking in the oven. Dry the eggplant completely before frying so it browns cleanly and does not cause excessive splattering.
history: A baked pasta specialty associated with Messina, Mistretta, and the Nebrodi, this dish layers pasta with ragù, fried eggplant, cheese, and other rich additions. Its name is commonly linked to an older covered-casserole cooking method using surrounding embers.

title: Pasta with Cuttlefish Ink
instructions:
Pasta with Cuttlefish Ink

Sicilian pasta with cuttlefish gently braised in its own ink, dry white wine, tomato paste, and chile.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

1 1/3 lb whole cuttlefish, about 2 medium, with ink sacs intact
3/4 lb linguine or spaghetti alla chitarra
2 tbsp tomato paste
1/4 cup dry white wine
1/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil
1 medium shallot or 1 fresh scallion
1 garlic clove
1 small red chile
1/3 cup plus 1 tbsp plus 1 tsp hot water
1/4 cup reserved pasta cooking water

For cooking the pasta
3 3/4 qt water
1 tbsp plus 1 tsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Clean the cuttlefish, keeping the ink sacs intact. Remove the cuttlebone, eyes, beak, and innards. Rinse the cuttlefish briefly and dry them.

2. Cut the bodies into thin strips and separate the tentacles.

3. Finely chop the shallot or scallion. Leave the chile whole for moderate heat or cut it into 4 pieces and retain the seeds for stronger heat.

4. Heat 3 tablespoons of the olive oil in a wide saucepan. Add the shallot, garlic, and chile and cook over low heat for 6 minutes.

5. Add 2 tablespoons of the hot water during the shallot cooking and continue until the shallot is translucent without browning.

6. Add the cuttlefish and sauté over medium heat for 3 minutes.

7. Pour in the wine and cook for 2 minutes, until the sharp alcohol aroma has diminished.

8. Stir in the tomato paste.

9. Carefully open the ink sacs and squeeze the ink into the saucepan. Add the remaining 1/4 cup plus 2 teaspoons hot water and stir until the ink is evenly dispersed.

10. Cover and cook over low heat for 15–20 minutes.

11. Bring the pasta water and salt to a boil. Cook the linguine until al dente, reserving 1/4 cup cooking water before draining.

12. Transfer the pasta to the saucepan with the cuttlefish. Add the remaining 1 tablespoon olive oil and the reserved pasta water.

13. Toss over medium heat for 1 minute, moving the pasta continuously until the black sauce coats it evenly.

Service

Divide among 4 plates and distribute the pieces of cuttlefish over and through the pasta.

Chef's note

Cuttlefish ink is naturally salty, so the measured salt is concentrated in the pasta water rather than added to the sauce. Gentle covered cooking keeps the cuttlefish tender and prevents the sauce from drying out.
history: This intensely colored seafood pasta is a longstanding Sicilian preparation built around fresh cuttlefish and its ink. Known in Sicilian as u niuru di siccia, it remains a classic of the island’s seafood cooking and is widely served in coastal restaurants.
description: Glossy black spaghetti carries the concentrated taste of cuttlefish, white wine, garlic, and tomato. Briny, savory, and striking on the plate, it offers a pure taste of the Mediterranean with dramatic color and deep marine richness.

title: Pasta with Trapanese Pesto
instructions:
Pasta with Trapanese Pesto

Busiate with a Trapani-style pesto of fresh tomato, almonds, Sicilian pecorino, red garlic, and basil.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

3 1/4 cups dry busiate
4 medium ripe tomatoes
1/2 cup blanched almonds
1/2 cup finely grated Sicilian pecorino
2 red garlic cloves
2 packed cups fresh basil leaves
1/4 cup plus 2 tsp extra-virgin olive oil
1 1/3 tsp fine salt
1 tsp freshly ground black pepper

For cooking the pasta
3 1/2 qt water
1 tbsp plus 2/3 tsp coarse salt
1 tbsp reserved pasta cooking water

Preparation

1. Cut a shallow X in the base of each tomato.

2. Lower the tomatoes into boiling water for 30–40 seconds, then transfer them to cold water.

3. Peel the tomatoes, cut them in half, and remove the seeds and excess interior liquid.

4. Spread the almonds on a baking sheet and toast them at 300°F for 15 minutes. Cool completely.

5. Put the almonds and garlic in a mortar. Pound until finely crushed but not completely smooth.

6. Add the tomatoes and pecorino and continue pounding until combined while retaining a slightly rustic texture.

7. Slowly work in the olive oil.

8. Add the basil, salt, and pepper only at the end. Pound for another 20–30 seconds, keeping the pesto slightly coarse.

9. Bring the water and coarse salt to a boil.

10. Cook the busiate until al dente. Before draining, measure and reserve 1 tablespoon of the cooking water.

11. Transfer the pasta to a large bowl, add the pesto and reserved cooking water.

12. Toss vigorously for 1 minute off the heat until the pesto is evenly distributed.

Service

Divide into 4 portions and serve immediately.

Chef's note

The pesto should remain slightly coarse. Prolonged processing warms the basil and almonds and makes the sauce too uniform; adding the basil only at the end helps preserve its aroma and color.
history: This Trapani specialty grew from contact with Genoese sailors who stopped at the western Sicilian port carrying agliata, a garlic-and-nut sauce. Trapanese cooks adapted the idea with local almonds, tomatoes, red garlic, basil, pecorino, and sea salt. Its regional identity remains firmly present at the table.
description: Busiate with a Trapani-style pesto of fresh tomato, almonds, Sicilian pecorino, red garlic, and basil.

title: Pasta with Fried Zucchini
instructions:
Pasta with Fried Zucchini

Sicilian spaghetti with fried pale-green zucchini, garlic, basil, mint, and ricotta salata.

Yield: 2 servings

Ingredients

7/16 lb spaghetti
1 large pale-green Sicilian zucchini
1 garlic clove, minced
8 fresh basil leaves
6 fresh mint leaves
1/3 cup finely grated ricotta salata
3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
3 1/4 cups extra-virgin olive oil or peanut oil for frying
1 2/3 tsp fine salt for the zucchini
1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper
1/4 cup reserved pasta cooking water

For cooking the pasta
2 1/8 qt water
2 1/3 tsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Trim the zucchini, peel it, and cut it into slices about 3/8 inch thick.

2. Layer the slices in a colander, distribute the 1 2/3 teaspoons salt over them, and rest for 30 minutes.

3. Rinse the slices briefly and dry them completely.

4. Heat the frying oil to 340°F. Fry the zucchini in batches until pale golden, about 2–3 minutes per side. Drain.

5. Heat the 3 tablespoons olive oil in a wide skillet over medium-low heat. Add the garlic and cook for 60 seconds without allowing it to brown.

6. Add the fried zucchini, 4 basil leaves, and 3 mint leaves torn into pieces. Toss for 30 seconds and remove the skillet from the heat.

7. Bring the water and salt to a boil. Cook the spaghetti until 2 minutes short of the package's stated cooking time.

8. Before draining, measure and reserve 1/4 cup of the pasta water.

9. Transfer the spaghetti to the skillet with the zucchini. Add the reserved pasta water and finish cooking for 2 minutes over medium heat, tossing continuously.

10. Turn off the heat. Add half of the ricotta salata and the black pepper and toss.

Service

Divide between 2 plates. Finish with the remaining ricotta salata and the remaining basil and mint leaves.

Chef's note

Keep the zucchini slices thick and only lightly golden rather than dark. Moderate browning preserves the soft texture and naturally sweet flavor of the pale-green Sicilian zucchini.
history: A traditional Sicilian summer pasta, this preparation centers on fried slices of pale-green zucchina napoletana, a seasonal variety prized locally. The classic approach is simple: spaghetti and fried zucchini, with later versions often adding herbs, garlic, and grated cheese. Its place at the table endures.
description: Sicilian spaghetti with fried pale-green zucchini, garlic, basil, mint, and ricotta salata.

instructions:
Pasta with Bottarga

Sicilian pasta with freshly grated tuna bottarga, garlic, chile, parsley, and extra-virgin olive oil.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

1 1/8 lb durum-wheat pasta

1/4 cup plus 2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil

For cooking the pasta
5 1/4 qt water
2 tbsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Bring the water and salt to a boil.

2. Cook the pasta until al dente and drain it.

3. Divide the parsley into two 1-tablespoon portions and the bottarga into two 1/4-cup portions.

4. Heat the olive oil in a wide skillet over medium-low heat.

5. Add the garlic, 1 tablespoon parsley, and the chile flakes. Cook for 2 minutes without browning the garlic.

6. Transfer the pasta to the skillet and toss it in the seasoned oil for 1 minute.

7. Turn off the heat completely.

8. Add the second tablespoon of parsley and 1/4 cup bottarga. Toss for 30 seconds.

9. Divide the pasta among 4 plates.

Service

Distribute 1 tablespoon of the remaining bottarga over each plate and serve immediately.

Chef's note

Add the bottarga only after the heat is turned off. The residual heat of the pasta is enough to release its aroma without muting its clean marine flavor.
history: Bottarga has deep Mediterranean roots; its name derives from Arabic butārikh, meaning salted fish roe. In Sicily, tuna bottarga is especially associated with places such as Favignana, Trapani, San Vito Lo Capo, and Marzamemi, where tuna preservation has long shaped coastal foodways. Its legacy endures.
description: Hot pasta is coated with garlic, olive oil, chili, parsley, and finely grated cured tuna roe added off the heat. Salty, marine, aromatic, and intensely savory, it delivers remarkable depth with a short ingredient list.

instructions:
Syracuse-style Pasta with Anchovies

Syracuse-style spaghetti with anchovies, chopped sun-dried tomato, capers, tomato extract, toasted breadcrumbs, peppered pecorino, and wild fennel.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

7/8 lb spaghetti
2 garlic cloves
8 oil-packed anchovy fillets
6 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil, divided
1/2 cup dry white wine
2 tbsp chopped sun-dried tomato
1 tbsp salt-packed capers, rinsed and dried
1 tbsp concentrated tomato paste
1/2 cup plus 1 tbsp dry breadcrumbs
1/2 cup finely grated peppered pecorino
1 small bunch wild fennel, finely chopped
1/2 cup reserved pasta cooking water

For cooking the pasta
4 1/4 qt water
1 tbsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Bring the water and salt to a boil.

2. Heat 1 tablespoon of the olive oil in a small skillet over medium-low heat. Add the breadcrumbs and toast for 4–5 minutes, stirring continuously, until golden. Transfer to a bowl.

3. Heat 4 tablespoons of the remaining olive oil in a wide skillet over medium-low heat. Add the minced garlic and cook for 60 seconds without browning it.

4. Add the anchovy fillets and stir for 2–3 minutes, until they dissolve into the oil.

5. Pour in the white wine. Increase the heat slightly and cook for 3 minutes, until the sharp alcohol aroma has largely cooked away.

6. Add the chopped sun-dried tomato and capers. Cook for 2 minutes.

7. Stir in the tomato paste and 1/4 cup of the reserved pasta water until the sauce is loose and even. Keep over low heat.

8. Cook the spaghetti until 2 minutes short of the package's stated cooking time. Before draining, reserve another 1/4 cup pasta water.

9. Transfer the spaghetti to the skillet. Add the remaining 1/4 cup pasta water gradually and toss over medium heat for 2 minutes.

10. Turn off the heat. Add half of the toasted breadcrumbs, half of the pecorino, and half of the chopped fennel. Toss for 30 seconds.

11. Divide among 4 plates.

Service

Finish each portion with the remaining breadcrumbs, pecorino, and fennel. Drizzle with the final 1 tablespoon olive oil.

Chef's note

Anchovies, capers, sun-dried tomato, and concentrated tomato paste all contribute saltiness. The measured salt therefore stays in the pasta water rather than being added separately to the sauce.
history: A Syracuse specialty, this anchovy-and-breadcrumb pasta reflects eastern Sicily’s pantry cooking, combining preserved fish, capers, concentrated tomato, pecorino, and wild fennel. Modern versions vary widely, but anchovies and toasted breadcrumbs remain defining features of the local tradition. Its regional identity remains firmly present at the table.
description: Syracuse-style spaghetti with anchovies, chopped sun-dried tomato, capers, tomato extract, toasted breadcrumbs, peppered pecorino, and wild fennel.

title: Sicilian Pasta with Cauliflower
instructions:
Sicilian Pasta with Cauliflower

Sicilian pasta with cauliflower, anchovies, currants, pine nuts, saffron, and onion.

Yield: 6 servings

Ingredients

1 1/3 lb bucato or small macaroni
1 medium-large cauliflower
4 salt-cured anchovies, rinsed and boned
3 tbsp dried currants
3 tbsp pine nuts
1 packet saffron
1 small onion, finely chopped
1/2 cup plus 1 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper
1/2 cup reserved cauliflower cooking water

For cooking the cauliflower and pasta
6 1/3 qt water
2 tbsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Put the currants and pine nuts in a bowl with 1 cup warm water. Soak for 20 minutes, then drain and dry.

2. Cut the cauliflower into evenly sized florets. Cut the tender part of the stalk into pieces as well.

3. Bring the water and salt to a boil.

4. Cook the cauliflower for 10–12 minutes, until tender but not falling apart. Lift it out with a slotted spoon and reserve all of the cooking water.

5. Dissolve the saffron in 1 tablespoon of the hot cauliflower cooking water.

6. Heat the olive oil in a wide pot over medium heat. Add the onion and cook for 6–8 minutes, until soft and lightly golden.

7. Add the currants and pine nuts and cook for 2 minutes.

8. Add the cauliflower and sauté over medium-high heat for 3 minutes. Mash about one-third of the florets with a wooden spoon so the sauce becomes creamy while the remaining cauliflower stays in pieces.

9. Add the dissolved saffron, the remaining reserved cauliflower water, and the black pepper. Cook over medium heat for 5 minutes.

10. Add the chopped anchovies and stir for 1 minute, until they dissolve into the sauce. Turn off the heat.

11. Return the cauliflower cooking water to a boil and cook the pasta until al dente.

12. Drain the pasta and transfer it to the pot with the sauce. Stir vigorously for 1 minute.

13. Transfer to a serving bowl and rest for 10 minutes.

Service

Divide into 6 portions and serve warm.

Chef's note

Mashing part of the cauliflower helps the sauce cling to the pasta while leaving some florets intact for texture. Adding the anchovies near the end preserves their savory flavor without drying them out.
history: A Palermo-style Sicilian tradition, this preparation uses cauliflower—the vegetable commonly called broccolo on the island—with onion, anchovies, raisins, pine nuts, and saffron. Related versions are known as pasta chi vruoccoli arriminati; arriminati refers to the vigorous mixing that breaks cauliflower into the sauce.
description: Tender cauliflower melts into a saffron-scented sauce with anchovies, sweet raisins, toasted pine nuts, and onion. The result is savory, gently sweet, nutty, and aromatic, with pasta absorbing every drop of the rich Sicilian-style dressing.

Orecchiette with Broccoli Rabe

Puglian orecchiette with broccoli rabe, anchovies, garlic, chile, and extra-virgin olive oil.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

3 cups dry orecchiette
2 large bunches broccoli rabe
4 oil-packed anchovy fillets
1/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil
1 garlic clove
1 small red chile

For cooking the pasta and greens
3 1/4 qt water
1 tbsp plus 1/2 tsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Trim away the tough parts of the broccoli rabe. Separate the tender leaves and florets and cut the tender stems into 1 1/4-inch pieces.

2. Bring the water and salt to a boil.

3. Add the leaves and tender stems and cook for 3–5 minutes.

4. Add the orecchiette and the more delicate florets. Cook together for 8–10 minutes, checking the pasta beginning at minute 7.

5. Meanwhile, heat the olive oil in a wide skillet over medium-low heat.

6. Add the crushed garlic, the chile split lengthwise, and the anchovy fillets.

7. Cook for 3–4 minutes, stirring until the anchovies dissolve into the oil. Remove the garlic.

8. Drain the orecchiette and broccoli rabe together when the pasta is al dente.

9. Transfer immediately to the skillet and toss over medium heat for 2 minutes, until the seasoning is evenly distributed.

Service

Divide among 4 plates and serve immediately.

Chef's note

Cooking the orecchiette and broccoli rabe in the same water allows the pasta to absorb the vegetable's flavor directly. The anchovies melt into the oil and provide much of the seasoning.
history: This combination is one of Puglia’s emblematic pasta dishes, especially associated with Bari. Its exact origin is uncertain. Regional tradition links the development of orecchiette to medieval Puglia, while pairing the hand-shaped pasta with locally abundant cime di rapa became a defining expression of the region’s cucina povera.
description: Chewy orecchiette capture garlicky olive oil, melted anchovy, chili, and pleasantly bitter turnip greens. The contrast is bold but balanced—peppery greens, savory fish, and rustic pasta combining into a deeply satisfying taste of southern Italy.

title: Barese Rice, Potato, and Mussel Tiella
instructions:
Barese Rice, Potato, and Mussel Tiella

Layered Bari-style casserole with Carnaroli rice, potatoes, mussels, Parmigiano, parsley, and breadcrumbs.

Yield: 6 servings

Ingredients

1 1/8 lb fresh mussels
1 1/8 lb potatoes
1 2/3 cups Carnaroli rice
1 1/4 cups water
1 garlic clove
1/2 cup dry breadcrumbs
2 cups loosely packed fresh parsley leaves
1/2 cup finely grated Parmigiano Reggiano
5 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
1 tsp fine salt
1 tsp freshly ground black pepper

Preparation

1. Clean the mussels thoroughly, removing the beards and any buildup from the shells.

2. Open the mussels raw with a small knife, collecting all of the liquid they release. Strain the liquid through a fine-mesh strainer. Keep each mussel attached to the lower shell and discard the upper shell.

3. Finely chop the garlic and parsley.

4. Mix the breadcrumbs with half of the chopped garlic and parsley and 2 tablespoons of the olive oil.

5. Peel the potatoes and cut them into slices about 1/8 inch thick.

6. Grease the bottom of a baking dish with 1 tablespoon olive oil.

7. Arrange half of the potatoes in the bottom. Season with one-third of the salt, one-quarter of the pepper, and one-quarter of the remaining parsley-garlic mixture.

8. Arrange half of the mussels over the potatoes with the meat facing upward.

9. Distribute half of the uncooked rice, half of the Parmigiano, and half of the strained mussel liquid over the layer.

10. Repeat with the remaining potatoes, mussels, and rice. Add another one-third of the salt, another one-quarter of the pepper, the remaining parsley-garlic mixture, the remaining Parmigiano, and the remaining mussel liquid.

11. Spread the seasoned breadcrumbs over the surface.

12. Pour the water slowly down the side of the baking dish without wetting the breadcrumb topping directly.

13. Finish with the remaining 2 tablespoons olive oil, the remaining salt, and the remaining pepper.

14. Bake on a lower oven rack at 350°F for 60 minutes, until the surface is golden and the rice has absorbed the liquid.

Service

Rest for 10 minutes, divide into 6 portions, and serve hot.

Chef's note

The strained mussel liquid is part of the cooking liquid and should not be discarded. Pouring the water around the edge keeps the topping dry enough to brown while the rice cooks in the liquid underneath.
history: A signature dish of Bari and Puglia, tiella takes its name from the baking vessel traditionally used to cook layered ingredients. The rice cooks by absorbing mussel liquor and added water rather than being stirred. The preparation is sometimes linked to culinary influences from Spanish rule in southern Italy.
description: Briny mussels, tender potatoes, and rice bake together in concentrated shellfish juices beneath a crisp breadcrumb-and-cheese crust. Each layer absorbs the one below it, creating a deeply savory, comforting casserole with the unmistakable flavor of the Adriatic coast.

title: Ciceri e Tria
instructions:
Ciceri e Tria

Salento-style chickpeas with fresh semolina pasta, with one-third of the pasta fried until crisp.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

For the chickpeas
2 cups dried chickpeas
8 1/2 cups cold water for soaking
6 1/3 cups fresh water for cooking
1 onion
1 celery stalk
1 carrot
2 bay leaves
2 tbsp plus 2 tsp extra-virgin olive oil
1 1/3 tsp fine salt
1 tsp freshly ground black pepper

For the tria
2 1/2 cups fine durum-wheat semolina
3/4 cup plus 1 tbsp plus 1 tsp warm water
2/3 tsp fine salt

For frying and finishing
2 cups plus 2 tbsp olive oil for frying
1 tbsp plus 1 tsp extra-virgin olive oil

Preparation

1. Put the chickpeas in a bowl with the soaking water and soak for 12 hours.

2. Drain and rinse the chickpeas.

3. Transfer them to a pot with the fresh cooking water, the halved onion, celery stalk, carrot, and bay leaves.

4. Bring to a gentle boil and cook over low heat for about 2 hours, until the chickpeas are tender but still intact.

5. Remove the onion, celery, carrot, and bay leaves. Add the olive oil, salt, and pepper. Cook for another 10 minutes over low heat.

6. Make the tria by combining the semolina with the salt.

7. Gradually add the warm water and knead vigorously until smooth and elastic.

8. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.

9. Roll the dough to about 1/16 inch thick and cut it into strips 1/2–3/4 inch wide and 4–6 inches long.

10. Divide the tria into two portions: one-third for frying and two-thirds for boiling.

11. Heat the frying oil to 350°F.

12. Fry the reserved one-third of the tria until golden and crisp. Drain on paper towels.

13. Return the chickpeas to a gentle boil. Add the unfried two-thirds of the tria and cook for 8–10 minutes.

14. Turn off the heat and stir in half of the fried tria.

15. Divide among 4 bowls.

Service

Top with the remaining fried tria and finish each serving with 1 teaspoon extra-virgin olive oil.

Chef's note

Adding the fried pasta in two stages preserves the contrast between soft and crisp tria. Make sure the pasta reserved for frying is dry on the surface before it enters the hot oil.
history: This Salento specialty belongs to Puglia’s long tradition of pasta and legumes. Its defining feature is frying part of the handmade tria while boiling the rest. The name preserves old Mediterranean language: ciceri echoes Latin cicer for chickpeas, while tria is commonly linked to an ancient term for pasta.
description: Creamy chickpeas surround handmade semolina ribbons while a portion of the pasta arrives golden and crisp on top. Soft, chewy, and crunchy textures meet in one bowl, enriched with olive oil and black pepper for deeply satisfying rustic comfort.

title: Orecchiette with Braciole Ragù
instructions:
Orecchiette with Braciole Ragù

Puglian orecchiette dressed with a slow-cooked tomato ragù made from veal rolls filled with pecorino, garlic, parsley, and cured pork fat.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

For the braciole and ragù
10 thin veal cutlets
about 1/2 lb cured pork fat, optional, divided
1 cup finely grated or shaved fresh pecorino, divided
1/4 cup finely chopped fresh parsley
10 fresh basil leaves
2 garlic cloves, finely minced
1 medium onion, finely chopped
1/4 cup plus 1 tsp extra-virgin olive oil
3/4 cup dry white wine
2 cups plus 2 tbsp rustic tomato sauce
1/4 tsp dried chile flakes
1 tsp fine salt
1 tsp freshly ground black pepper
1 cup hot water

For the pasta
7/8 lb fresh durum-wheat orecchiette
4 1/4 qt water
1 tbsp plus 1 1/2 tsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Gently pound the veal cutlets between sheets of parchment until they are an even 1/8 inch thick.

2. Reserve 1/3 cup of the pecorino for serving. Divide the remaining pecorino, garlic, parsley, half of the chile, about 1/4 lb of the finely chopped cured pork fat, 1/3 teaspoon salt, and 1/2 teaspoon pepper among the cutlets.

3. Roll each cutlet tightly and secure it with kitchen twine or a toothpick.

4. Heat the olive oil in a heavy pot over medium heat. Add the onion and the remaining cured pork fat, if using. Cook for 6 minutes, until the onion is soft.

5. Add the braciole and brown for 8–10 minutes, turning until well colored on all sides.

6. Pour in the white wine and cook for 3 minutes, until the sharp alcohol aroma has largely cooked away.

7. Add the tomato sauce, basil, remaining chile, remaining salt, and remaining pepper. Bring to a gentle simmer.

8. Reduce the heat to low, cover with the lid slightly ajar, and cook for about 2 hours. Stir every 20 minutes. If the sauce becomes too thick before the meat is tender, add the hot water in 1/4-cup portions, using no more than 1 cup total.

9. When the braciole are tender and the sauce is thick but still fluid, transfer the rolls to a warm plate and cover. Remove the twine or toothpicks before serving.

10. Bring the pasta water and salt to a boil. Cook the orecchiette until al dente and drain.

11. Toss the orecchiette immediately with a generous amount of ragù over low heat for 1 minute.

Service

Divide among 4 plates and finish with the reserved pecorino. Serve the braciole separately as the second course with additional ragù.

Chef's note

Keep the ragù at a slow simmer. Vigorous boiling can toughen the meat and reduce the sauce too quickly. Add the measured hot water only during the long braise when needed to keep the sauce fluid enough to coat the pasta.
history: A cornerstone of Puglian Sunday lunch, especially in Bari, this preparation pairs orecchiette with tomato sauce from slowly braised stuffed meat rolls. Older Barese tradition often used horse meat; today beef or veal is common. The braciole are traditionally served after the pasta as a second course.
description: Hand-shaped orecchiette catch a deep tomato sauce enriched by slow-braised stuffed meat rolls, pecorino, garlic, parsley, and wine. Rich, savory, and celebratory, the meal delivers both a luxurious pasta course and tender rolled meat for the table.

title: Puglian Baked Macaroni
instructions:
Puglian Baked Macaroni

Puglian baked pasta with tomato sauce, tiny meatballs, mozzarella, mortadella, Parmigiano, Pecorino Romano, and breadcrumbs.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

For the tomato sauce
4 1/4 cups tomato sauce
1 medium onion, finely chopped
2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
1 tsp fine salt
10 fresh basil leaves

For the meatballs
scant 1/2 lb mixed ground veal and pork
1/3 cup dry breadcrumbs
1 cup finely grated Pecorino Romano
2 tbsp whole milk
1 large egg
2/3 tsp fine salt
2 cups plus 2 tbsp peanut oil for frying

For assembly
1 1/8 lb ziti or penne
1 1/8 lb well-drained mozzarella, diced
1 cup finely grated Parmigiano Reggiano
about 1/4 lb sliced mortadella
1/4 cup dry breadcrumbs
2 San Marzano tomatoes, halved and gently crushed

For cooking the pasta
5 1/4 qt water
2 tbsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Make the tomato sauce. Heat the olive oil in a saucepan over medium-low heat. Add the onion and cook for 6 minutes, until soft without browning.

2. Add the tomato sauce, 1 teaspoon salt, and 6 basil leaves. Cook uncovered over low heat for 30 minutes.

3. Make the meatballs. Combine the ground meat, 1/3 cup breadcrumbs, Pecorino Romano, milk, egg, and 2/3 teaspoon salt until evenly mixed.

4. Shape into cherry-size meatballs about 3/4 inch in diameter.

5. Heat the peanut oil to 350°F. Fry the meatballs in batches for 2–3 minutes, until golden. Drain on paper towels.

6. Transfer the meatballs to the tomato sauce and cook over low heat for 10 minutes.

7. Bring the pasta water and salt to a boil. Cook the ziti or penne until 3 minutes short of the package's stated cooking time. Drain.

8. Toss the pasta with about one-third of the sauce and 1/3 cup of the Parmigiano.

9. Preheat the oven to 350°F.

10. Spread a thin layer of sauce over the bottom of a baking dish. Add half of the pasta.

11. Distribute half of the mozzarella, all of the mortadella, all of the meatballs, another 1/3 cup Parmigiano, and additional sauce over the pasta.

12. Cover with the remaining pasta. Top with the remaining sauce, remaining mozzarella, and remaining 1/3 cup Parmigiano.

13. Arrange the 4 San Marzano tomato halves over the surface, add the remaining 4 basil leaves, and distribute the 1/4 cup breadcrumbs evenly over the top.

14. Bake at 350°F for 10 minutes.

15. Switch the oven to broil and brown for another 5 minutes, watching continuously, until the top is deeply golden and crisp.

16. Rest for 10 minutes before serving.

Service

Divide into 4 portions and serve hot.

Chef's note

The pasta should go into the oven decidedly al dente because it absorbs more sauce during the final bake. Thoroughly draining the mozzarella keeps excess liquid from collecting in the bottom of the dish.
history: Baked pasta is a Sunday and holiday staple across southern Italy. In Puglia, especially Bari, versions often become lavish with tiny meatballs, mozzarella or scamorza, mortadella, and grated cheese. The dish reflects family cooking designed to combine pasta, sauce, meat, and cheese in one celebratory bake.
description: Layers of tomato-coated penne, tiny fried meatballs, melting mozzarella, mortadella, and aged cheeses bake beneath a crisp breadcrumb crust. It is generous, gooey, deeply savory comfort food with browned edges and a rich center made for sharing.

title: Seafood Linguine in Foil Packets
instructions:
Seafood Linguine in Foil Packets

Seafood linguine finished in individual foil packets with cherry tomatoes, white wine, cream, and butter.

Yield: 6 servings

Ingredients

1 1/8 lb linguine
2 1/4 lb fresh mussels
1 1/8 lb littleneck or Manila clams
6 medium shrimp
about 1/2 lb cleaned cuttlefish, cut into strips
1 1/4 cups diced cherry tomatoes
2 garlic cloves, minced
3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
3/4 cup dry white wine
1/2 cup cooking cream
2 tbsp unsalted butter
3/4 tsp fine salt
6 sheets aluminum foil, each about 18 inches long

For cooking the pasta
5 1/4 qt water
1 tbsp plus 2 tsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Purge the clams in cold salted water for 2 hours, then rinse thoroughly. Scrub and debeard the mussels. Rinse the shrimp and cuttlefish and pat dry.

2. Put the mussels and clams in a wide pot, cover, and cook over medium-high heat for 4–5 minutes, removing each shellfish as it opens. Discard any that remain closed.

3. Strain the shellfish liquid carefully through a fine-mesh strainer lined with cheesecloth or a clean paper towel. Reserve 3/4 cup of the strained liquid.

4. Remove about two-thirds of the mussels and clams from their shells, leaving the remainder in their shells for the packets.

5. Heat the olive oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Add the garlic and cook for 60 seconds.

6. Add the cuttlefish and cook for 3 minutes. Add the shrimp and cook for another 2 minutes.

7. Pour in the white wine and cook for 3 minutes, until the sharp alcohol aroma has largely cooked away.

8. Add the cherry tomatoes and fine salt. Cover and cook for 8 minutes.

9. Add the reserved shellfish liquid, mussels, and clams. Cook uncovered for 3 minutes, then turn off the heat.

10. Bring the pasta water and salt to a boil. Cook the linguine until 4 minutes short of the package's stated cooking time. Drain.

11. Transfer the linguine to the seafood pan. Add the cream and toss over medium-low heat for 1 minute.

12. Preheat the oven to 320°F.

13. Lay the 6 sheets of foil on the work surface. Put 1 teaspoon butter in the center of each sheet.

14. Divide the linguine, seafood, and sauce evenly among the foil sheets. Bring the sides of each sheet upward and seal the packet, leaving a little interior space for steam.

15. Arrange the packets on a baking sheet and bake for 8 minutes.

Service

Bring the packets to the table closed and open them carefully just before eating.

Chef's note

Drain the pasta very al dente because it finishes cooking inside the packet. The strained mussel and clam liquid intensifies the seafood flavor and keeps the sauce fluid without diluting it with plain water.
history: Cooking seafood pasta al cartoccio became popular in central and southern Italian restaurant cooking: very al dente pasta and sauce are sealed in foil or parchment and finished in the oven. The packet traps steam and shellfish aromas, then opens dramatically at the table.
description: A sealed parcel opens to release a rush of seafood, garlic, white wine, tomato, cream, and butter around tender linguine. The brief oven finish concentrates the sauce and perfumes every strand before the packet reaches the table.

title: Linguine with Cuttlefish Ragù
instructions:
Linguine with Cuttlefish Ragù

Neapolitan-style linguine with browned cuttlefish, dry white wine, and tomato.

Yield: 2 servings

Ingredients

7/16 lb linguine
1 medium cuttlefish, cleaned
1 cup crushed peeled tomatoes or peeled cherry tomatoes
2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
1 garlic clove
1/4 cup dry white wine
1/2 tsp fine salt

For cooking the pasta
2 1/8 qt water
2 1/3 tsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Wash the cuttlefish thoroughly. Remove the cuttlebone, eyes, beak, skin, innards, and ink sac. Rinse briefly and pat dry.

2. Cut the body into roughly 3/4-inch squares and cut the tentacles into similar-size pieces.

3. Heat the olive oil in a wide saucepan over medium heat. Add the whole garlic clove and cook for 1–2 minutes, until golden. Remove the garlic.

4. Add the cuttlefish and sauté over medium-high heat for 2 minutes.

5. Pour in the white wine and cook for 2 minutes, until the sharp alcohol aroma has largely cooked away.

6. Add the crushed tomatoes and 1/2 teaspoon salt. Cook over high heat for 5 minutes.

7. Reduce the heat, cover partially, and cook for 18–20 minutes, stirring every 5 minutes, until the cuttlefish is tender and the sauce is cohesive.

8. Bring the pasta water and salt to a boil. Cook the linguine until 1 minute short of the package's stated cooking time.

9. Drain the linguine and transfer it directly to the cuttlefish ragù.

10. Toss over high heat for 1 minute, stirring continuously until the sauce coats the pasta evenly.

Service

Divide between 2 plates and distribute the cuttlefish pieces over the linguine. Serve immediately.

Chef's note

The cuttlefish is first browned briefly and then cooked gently in the tomato. The final 1-minute toss finishes the pasta without unnecessarily extending the cooking time of the cuttlefish.
history: Cuttlefish ragù belongs to Italy’s coastal seafood tradition, particularly in southern regions where seppia is simmered with garlic, wine, and tomato before dressing pasta. Unlike ink-based preparations, the emphasis is tender cuttlefish and the concentrated tomato-seafood sauce created during cooking.
description: Tender cuttlefish simmers with garlic, white wine, and tomato until the sauce turns rich and ocean-sweet, then clings to long linguine. The result is comforting yet distinctly coastal, with deep savory flavor and a clean Mediterranean finish.

title: Lagane with Chickpeas
instructions:
Lagane with Chickpeas

Lucanian fresh lagane pasta with chickpeas and crisp Senise peppers.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

For the chickpeas
1 1/4 cups dried chickpeas
6 1/3 cups water for soaking
6 1/3 cups fresh water for cooking
1 bay leaf
3/4 tsp fine salt

For the lagane
1 7/8 cups durum-wheat flour
1 2/3 cups all-purpose flour
2 large eggs
3/4 cup plus 1 tbsp plus 1 tsp warm water
2/3 tsp fine salt

For the sauce
1 garlic clove
1/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil, divided
4 Senise dried sweet peppers
1/3 tsp fine salt
1/2 cup reserved chickpea cooking liquid

For cooking the lagane
4 1/4 qt water
1 tbsp plus 1 1/2 tsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Rinse the chickpeas and soak them in the cold water for 12 hours.

2. Drain and rinse the chickpeas. Transfer them to a pot with the fresh water and bay leaf. Bring to a gentle boil and cook over low heat for 90–120 minutes, until tender but still intact.

3. Add the 3/4 teaspoon salt during the final 15 minutes. Before draining the chickpeas, reserve 1/2 cup of their cooking liquid. Discard the bay leaf.

4. Make the lagane. Combine the durum-wheat flour and all-purpose flour on the work surface and form a well.

5. Add the eggs, warm water, and 2/3 teaspoon salt to the well. Knead for 10 minutes, until smooth and uniform.

6. Cover and rest for 10 minutes.

7. Roll the dough with a rolling pin to about 1/16 inch thick. Loosely roll the sheet onto itself and cut it into strips about 3/4 inch wide. Unroll the strips immediately, dust them lightly with flour, and dry for 15 minutes.

8. Wipe the dried Senise peppers with a dry cloth, remove the stems and seeds, and cut each pepper into 2–3 pieces.

9. Heat 2 tablespoons of the olive oil in a small skillet over medium heat. Fry the pepper pieces for only 5–10 seconds per side, just until glossy and crisp. Remove immediately and drain on paper towels; they will become crisper as they cool.

10. Heat the remaining 2 tablespoons olive oil in a wide skillet. Add the whole garlic clove and cook for 1–2 minutes, until golden. Remove the garlic.

11. Add the cooked chickpeas, 1/3 teaspoon salt, and reserved chickpea liquid. Cook over medium-low heat for 8 minutes, mashing about one-quarter of the chickpeas with the back of a spoon to create a creamy base.

12. Bring the pasta water and salt to a boil. Cook the fresh lagane for 3–4 minutes, until tender but still firm.

13. Drain the lagane and transfer them directly to the skillet with the chickpeas. Toss over medium heat for 1 minute.

14. Coarsely crumble half of the crisp peppers and fold them into the pasta. Turn off the heat.

Service

Divide among 4 plates and finish with the remaining crisp peppers.

Chef's note

The dried Senise peppers need only a few seconds in hot oil; longer frying makes them dark and bitter. Mashing a small portion of the chickpeas creates a natural sauce that binds the lagane without adding other ingredients.
history: A traditional Basilicata dish, this preparation is also associated with the nickname “brigands’ dish.” Regional oral tradition says 19th-century brigands in the Gallipoli Cognato woods were called mangialagane for their appetite for the broad handmade pasta. Chickpeas and Senise peppers anchor this Lucanian version.
description: Broad handmade ribbons meet creamy chickpeas, fragrant garlic, and bay, then gain a brilliant crackle from quickly fried sweet red peppers. Earthy, rustic, and deeply comforting, it combines soft legumes, chewy pasta, and crisp smoky-sweet contrast.

title: Strascinati with Peperoni Cruschi
instructions:
Strascinati with Peperoni Cruschi

Fresh Lucanian pasta from the Pollino area with crisp dried peppers, stale breadcrumbs, garlic, parsley, and extra-virgin olive oil.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

For the strascinati
2 cups durum-wheat flour
1/2 cup warm water
3/4 tsp fine salt

For the sauce
about 1/6 lb peperoni cruschi
1 1/2 cups coarse stale breadcrumbs
6 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
2 garlic cloves
3/4 tsp fine salt
1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper
1/4 cup finely chopped fresh parsley

For cooking the pasta
4 1/4 qt water
1 tbsp plus 1 1/2 tsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Mound the durum-wheat flour on the work surface and form a well.

2. Dissolve the 3/4 teaspoon salt in the warm water and add it gradually to the flour.

3. Knead for 10 minutes, until the dough is smooth and firm.

4. Cover and rest for 20 minutes.

5. Break the peperoni cruschi into roughly 1-inch pieces and remove the seeds.

6. Heat 5 tablespoons of the olive oil in a skillet over medium-low heat.

7. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute.

8. Add the stale breadcrumbs and toast for 4–5 minutes, stirring continuously, until crisp and golden.

9. Add the peperoni cruschi, 3/4 teaspoon salt, and black pepper. Cook over low heat for 2 minutes, then turn off the heat.

10. Divide the dough into pieces about 2 teaspoons each. Drag each piece across the work surface with two fingers to create the characteristic hollowed shape.

11. Bring the pasta water and salt to a boil.

12. Cook the strascinati until they float, then continue cooking for another 3 minutes.

13. Lift them out with a slotted spoon and transfer directly to the skillet with the breadcrumbs and peppers.

14. Toss over medium heat for 1 minute.

15. Turn off the heat and add the parsley and remaining 1 tablespoon olive oil.

Service

Divide among 4 plates and serve immediately.

Chef's note

Keep the breadcrumbs crisp and do not allow the peperoni cruschi to darken. Adding the peppers only during the final 2 minutes protects their characteristic sweet, toasted flavor.
history: In the Pollino area of Basilicata, strascinati and peperoni cruschi embody rural Lucanian cooking. The pasta is shaped by dragging dough across a board; sun-dried sweet peppers become crisp when heated, while stale bread crumb reflects a cucina povera tradition built around preserved local staples.
description: Hand-dragged pasta meets brittle sweet red peppers, garlicky toasted bread, parsley, and fruity olive oil. Crisp crumbs and smoky-sweet pepper flakes contrast with chewy fresh pasta, creating a rustic, intensely regional plate with remarkable texture.

title: Cavatelli with Peperoni Cruschi and Fried Breadcrumbs
instructions:
Cavatelli with Peperoni Cruschi and Fried Breadcrumbs

Lucanian cavatelli with tomato sauce, crisp dried peppers, and breadcrumbs toasted in the pepper-scented oil.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

3/4 lb cavatelli
10 dried peperoni cruschi
1 1/4 cups tomato passata
1 1/2 cups coarse fresh breadcrumbs
1 garlic clove
3 tbsp plus 1 tsp water
4 fresh basil leaves
6 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
3/4 tsp fine salt
1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper
1/2 cup reserved pasta cooking water

For cooking the cavatelli
3 3/4 qt water
1 tbsp plus 1 tsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Wipe the 10 peperoni cruschi with a dry cloth.

2. Heat 4 tablespoons olive oil in a wide skillet over moderate heat.

3. Add the peppers and cook over low heat for 2 minutes, turning continuously. Remove them from the oil and cool.

4. Once crisp, remove the stems and seeds. Keep the pepper-infused oil in the skillet.

5. Heat the remaining 2 tablespoons olive oil in a saucepan. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute, then remove it.

6. Add the passata, water, and basil. Cook over medium-low heat for 8 minutes.

7. Crumble the peperoni cruschi into the tomato sauce. Add the fine salt and black pepper and cook for another 5 minutes.

8. Return the skillet containing the pepper-infused oil to the heat. Add the breadcrumbs and toast for 4 minutes, stirring continuously. Transfer to paper towels.

9. Bring the pasta water and salt to a boil.

10. Cook the cavatelli for 7 minutes. Before draining, reserve 1/2 cup cooking water.

11. Transfer the cavatelli to the saucepan with the pepper sauce and add the reserved cooking water.

12. Toss over medium heat for 2 minutes.

Service

Divide among 4 plates and add the fried breadcrumbs only at the moment of serving.

Chef's note

Toasting the breadcrumbs in the oil used for the peppers carries their aroma into the crunchy topping. Adding the crumbs only after plating preserves the contrast in texture.
history: Peperoni cruschi are a defining ingredient of Basilicata, especially the thin-walled peppers associated with Senise that are dried and briefly fried until crisp. Pairing them with cavatelli and fried bread crumb reflects Lucanian cucina povera, where durable pantry staples become intensely flavored pasta dishes.
description: Tender cavatelli carry a bright tomato sauce scented with garlic and sweet dried peppers, while crisp fried bread crumbs add a deep toasted crunch. The combination is rustic, vivid, and layered with the smoky sweetness of Basilicata’s celebrated peppers.

title: Pasta with Breadcrumbs and Fresh Anchovies
instructions:
Pasta with Breadcrumbs and Fresh Anchovies

Calabrian spaghetti with fresh anchovies, stale breadcrumbs, garlic, chile, parsley, and extra-virgin olive oil.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

about 3/4 lb spaghetti

4 garlic cloves, minced
1 fresh red chile, finely chopped
1/3 cup extra-virgin olive oil

For cooking the pasta
3 3/4 qt water
1 tbsp plus 1 tsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Clean the anchovies by removing the heads, innards, and center bones. Rinse briefly and pat dry.

2. Heat 1/4 cup of the olive oil in a large skillet.

3. Add the garlic and chile. Cook over medium-low heat for 1 minute.

4. Add the anchovies and cook for 3 minutes, breaking them apart with a fork.

5. Add the breadcrumbs and toast them in the anchovy mixture for 5 minutes, stirring continuously, until golden and crisp.

6. Bring the pasta water and salt to a boil.

7. Cook the spaghetti until 2 minutes short of the minimum package cooking time.

8. Drain and transfer the spaghetti to the skillet with the anchovies and breadcrumbs.

9. Toss over medium heat for 2 minutes until the coating is evenly distributed.

10. Turn off the heat. Add the parsley and remaining 1 tablespoon plus 1 teaspoon olive oil.

Service

Divide among 4 plates and serve immediately.

Chef's note

The toasted breadcrumbs take the place of grated cheese and should be distinctly golden without burning. Their crisp texture is essential against the soft anchovies.
history: A traditional dish of Calabria’s Tyrrhenian coast, this pasta grew from both fishing and cucina povera traditions. Anchovies supplied affordable protein, while stale bread crumb prevented waste and replaced costly grated cheese. In Cosenza province, versions are traditionally included among the Christmas Eve courses.
description: Fresh anchovies melt into garlic and chili while coarse stale bread turns deeply golden and crisp. Tossed through spaghetti with parsley and olive oil, the result is briny, crunchy, fragrant, and rooted in resourceful coastal cooking.

title: Calabrian Baked Pasta and Potatoes
instructions:
Calabrian Baked Pasta and Potatoes

Calabrian baked pasta with Sila potatoes, ziti, tomato, Caciocavallo Silano, breadcrumbs, and fresh chile.

1 3/4 lb Sila potatoes

1 fresh red chile, finely chopped

3/4 tsp fine salt

For precooking
5 1/4 qt water
2 tbsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Heat 3 tablespoons olive oil in a skillet.

2. Add the garlic and sauté for 1 minute.

3. Add the passata, basil, chile, and 3/4 teaspoon salt.

4. Cook over low heat for 20 minutes, stirring every 4 minutes.

5. Peel the potatoes and cut them into slices about 1/8 inch thick.

6. Bring the water and salt to a boil.

7. Add the potatoes and cook for 5 minutes.

8. Break the ziti in half, add them to the pot, and cook the potatoes and pasta together for another 5 minutes.

9. Drain completely.

10. Toss with about 1 2/3 cups of the tomato sauce.

11. Transfer to a large baking dish. Distribute the Caciocavallo, remaining sauce, and breadcrumbs over the pasta and potatoes.

12. Drizzle the remaining 1 tablespoon olive oil over the surface.

13. Bake in a preheated 400°F oven for 30 minutes.

14. Switch to broil for 3 minutes, until the surface is golden.

15. Rest for 10 minutes before serving.

Service

Divide into 4–6 portions and serve hot.

Chef's note

The potatoes and ziti receive only 10 minutes of total precooking in water. They finish in the oven, where the potato starch helps bind the pasta, tomato, and cheese.
history: Known in the Cosenza area as ara tijeddra, this Calabrian pasta-and-potato bake was traditionally assembled in a terracotta pan and cooked in the residual heat of a wood-fired bread oven. Its inexpensive ingredients made it a substantial expression of local cucina povera. Its legacy endures.
description: Tender Sila potatoes and ziti bake with tomato, garlic, chili, caciocavallo, and crisp bread crumb. The potatoes release starch as the cheese melts, creating a hearty, cohesive casserole with creamy interiors and a deeply browned top.

title: Pasta alla Jonica
instructions:
Pasta alla Jonica

Calabrian spaghetti with tomato, bell peppers, guanciale, basil, and pecorino.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

13/16 lb spaghetti
1 1/2 cups chopped fresh tomatoes
1/4 lb guanciale
2 bell peppers
2 garlic cloves
8 fresh basil leaves
1/2 cup finely grated pecorino
2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
1/2 tsp fine salt

For cooking the spaghetti
4 1/4 qt water
1 tbsp plus 1 tsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Wash the tomatoes and bell peppers.

2. Cut the tomatoes into 3/4-inch pieces and the peppers into strips about 3/8 inch wide.

3. Heat 1 tablespoon olive oil in a skillet. Add the tomatoes and peppers and cook over medium heat for 8 minutes.

4. Pass the cooked tomatoes and peppers through a food mill to make a smooth sauce.

5. Heat the remaining 1 tablespoon olive oil in a second skillet.

6. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute, then remove it.

7. Cut the guanciale into roughly 3/8-inch cubes. Add it to the skillet and brown for 5 minutes.

8. Pour in the tomato-pepper sauce. Add the basil and 1/2 teaspoon salt.

9. Cook over medium heat for 4 minutes.

10. Bring the pasta water and salt to a boil.

11. Cook the spaghetti until 2 minutes short of the minimum package cooking time.

12. Drain and transfer the spaghetti to the skillet with the sauce.

13. Toss over high heat for 2 minutes.

Service

Divide among 4 plates and top each portion with 2 tablespoons finely grated pecorino.

Chef's note

Passing the tomatoes and peppers through a food mill creates a smooth sauce that clings evenly to the spaghetti. Browning the guanciale separately keeps its texture distinct.
history: This is documented in Calabrian regional cooking collections as a traditional first course rather than a dish with a known inventor or fixed creation date. Its combination of peppers, fresh tomato, guanciale, basil, garlic, and pecorino reflects characteristic ingredients of Calabria’s robust pasta cooking.
description: Silky tomato-and-pepper sauce coats spaghetti while browned guanciale adds smoky richness and pecorino brings a salty finish. Garlic and basil keep the dish aromatic, balancing sweet vegetables with cured pork in a bold, satisfying plate.

title: Fileja with ’Nduja
instructions:
Fileja with ’Nduja

Calabrian fileja with ’nduja, Tropea red onion, tomato, and fresh parsley.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

1 medium Tropea red onion, thinly sliced
2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
about 1/6 lb Calabrian ’nduja
1 2/3 cups crushed peeled tomatoes
1/3 tsp fine salt
about 3/4 lb Calabrian fileja
3 1/4 qt water
1 tbsp plus 1 tsp coarse salt
3 tbsp finely chopped fresh parsley
2/3 cup pasta cooking water to reserve

Preparation

1. Thinly slice the Tropea onion.

2. Heat the olive oil in a large skillet over low heat.

3. Add the onion and cook for 6–7 minutes, stirring regularly, without browning.

4. Add the ’nduja in small pieces and stir over low heat for 2 minutes, until it melts into the cooking fat.

5. Crush the peeled tomatoes and add them to the skillet.

6. Add the fine salt and cook over medium-low heat for 18–20 minutes.

7. Bring the water to a boil and add the coarse salt.

8. Cook the fileja. Drain it 1–2 minutes before the stated cooking time ends, reserving 2/3 cup pasta water.

9. Transfer the fileja to the skillet with the sauce.

10. Add 3 tablespoons plus 1 teaspoon of the reserved pasta water and toss for 1–2 minutes.

11. Remove from the heat and fold in the chopped parsley.

12. Rest in the skillet for 1 minute.

Service

Divide among 4 plates and serve immediately.

Chef's note

Melt the ’nduja over low heat before adding the tomato. The fileja finishes cooking in the sauce with a measured amount of starchy pasta water, which binds the sauce without diluting its flavor.
history: Fileja is a handmade pasta of Vibo Valentia, traditionally wrapped around a thin reed or ferretto. ’Nduja comes from Spilinga on Monte Poro, where pork and Calabrian chile are cured into a soft salume. Their pairing is now one of the Vibonese area’s most recognizable pasta preparations.
description: Twisted handmade pasta catches a fiery tomato sauce enriched with melting cured pork, sweet Tropea onion, and fresh parsley. Spicy, savory, and deeply Calabrian, every groove holds the rich sauce while the onion softens the chile’s intensity.

title: Calabrian Homemade Maccarruni with Pork Ragù
instructions:
Calabrian Homemade Maccarruni with Pork Ragù

Hand-shaped Calabrian ferretto macaroni with a slow pork, liver-sausage, and tomato ragù.

Yield: 8 servings

Ingredients

For the maccarruni
6 1/4 cups durum-wheat flour
1 large egg
1 2/3 cups warm water
1 tsp extra-virgin olive oil
1 1/3 tsp fine salt

For the Calabrian ragù
scant 1/2 lb lean pork, cut into cubes
scant 1/2 lb pork ribs, cut into small pieces
scant 1/2 lb pork liver sausage
3 1/3 cups chopped tomatoes
3 1/2 tbsp lard
1 garlic clove, minced
1/4 cup finely chopped fresh parsley
1/2 onion, finely chopped
1/2 carrot, finely chopped
1/2 celery stalk, finely chopped
1/3 cup plus 1 tbsp dry white wine
1/3 cup plus 1 tbsp meat broth
1 hot red chile, crumbled
1 tsp fine salt

For cooking the pasta
8 1/2 qt water
2 tbsp plus 2 tsp fine salt
1 tbsp olive oil

Preparation

1. Make the ragù. Heat half of the lard in a heavy pot. Prick the liver sausages in several places and brown them for 5 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

2. Add the remaining lard, lean pork, and ribs to the pot. Brown over medium-high heat for 8 minutes.

3. Add the garlic, parsley, onion, carrot, and celery. Cook for 6 minutes, stirring.

4. Add the fine salt and chile. Pour in the white wine and cook for 3 minutes, until the sharp alcohol aroma has largely cooked away.

5. Add the tomatoes, broth, and browned sausages. Bring to a gentle simmer.

6. Reduce the heat and cook uncovered for at least 60 minutes, stirring every 15 minutes, until the meat is tender and the sauce is concentrated.

7. Make the maccarruni. Mound the durum-wheat flour on the work surface and form a well.

8. Dissolve the salt in the warm water. Add the egg, olive oil, and about three-quarters of the water to the well.

9. Gradually incorporate the flour, adding the remaining water as you knead. Knead for 12 minutes, until the dough is smooth, firm, and no longer sticky.

10. Wrap the dough in a clean kitchen towel that has been dampened with cold water and wrung out thoroughly. Rest for 10 minutes.

11. Pinch off small pieces and roll them into sticks about 2 3/4 inches long and 1/4 inch thick.

12. Spiral each piece around a thin ferretto or knitting needle. Roll gently with both hands to lengthen it without flattening, then slide out the rod.

13. Arrange the macaroni well apart on a floured cloth and dry for 60 minutes.

14. Bring the water, salt, and olive oil to a boil.

15. Cook the fresh maccarruni in batches for 5–7 minutes, depending on thickness, until cooked through but still firm.

16. Drain and dress immediately with the Calabrian ragù.

Service

Divide among 8 plates and spoon a generous amount of ragù over each serving. Serve the meat from the ragù alongside the pasta or on top.

Chef's note

The dough needs to be firm enough to slide cleanly off the ferretto without collapsing. Dry the shaped macaroni well separated before boiling, while the ragù should simmer gently until the pork is tender and the tomato has concentrated.
history: Known across Calabria as maccarruni i casa or maccheroni al ferretto, these handmade hollow noodles are shaped around a thin rod, reed, or knitting needle. In Reggio Calabria and elsewhere, they are traditionally paired with substantial meat sauces, especially pork ragù, for Sundays and celebrations.
description: Hand-rolled hollow noodles grip a long-simmered pork ragù in every groove and channel. The chewy fresh pasta and concentrated tomato-meat sauce create a rustic Sunday centerpiece built for grated cheese, generous portions, and slow family meals.

title: Linguine di Aspromonte
instructions:
Linguine di Aspromonte

Calabrian linguine with eggplant, zucchini, bell peppers, mushrooms, tomato, celery, and fresh herbs.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

3/4 lb linguine
2 medium eggplants
2 medium zucchini
4 mixed green, yellow, and red bell peppers
2 cups sliced porcini or cremini mushrooms
2 cups chopped fresh or canned peeled tomatoes
1 medium onion, sliced very thin
4 garlic cloves
1 celery stalk, finely chopped
1/4 cup finely chopped fresh parsley
10 fresh basil leaves
1 small red chile, finely chopped
2 cups plus 2 tbsp olive oil for frying
1/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil for the sauce
1 cup water
1 tbsp plus 1/3 tsp fine salt for the eggplant
3/4 tsp fine salt for the sauce

For cooking the linguine
4 1/4 qt water
1 tbsp plus 1 tsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Cut the unpeeled eggplants into roughly 3/4-inch cubes. Put them in a colander, distribute the salt for the eggplant evenly, cover with a plate and a weight, and press for 30 minutes.

2. Rinse the eggplant thoroughly and dry it completely.

3. Cut the zucchini into rounds about 1/4 inch thick.

4. Heat the frying oil to 340°F. Fry the eggplant in batches for 3–4 minutes, until soft and only lightly golden. Drain on paper towels.

5. Fry the zucchini in the same oil for 2–3 minutes, until tender and golden at the edges. Drain and reserve.

6. Heat the extra-virgin olive oil for the sauce in a wide pot. Add the onion and 1/2 cup water. Cook over low heat for 20 minutes, until the onion is very soft.

7. Add the garlic and cook for 30 seconds, then remove it.

8. Cut the bell peppers into roughly 3/4-inch pieces. Add them to the onion with the remaining 1/2 cup water and cook for 10 minutes.

9. Add the mushrooms and parsley. Cook over medium heat for 12 minutes.

10. Add the tomatoes, celery, basil, chile, and fine salt for the sauce. Cook over medium-low heat for 30 minutes.

11. Add the fried eggplant and cook for another 10 minutes. Keep the fried zucchini separate until the finish.

12. Bring the pasta water and salt to a boil. Cook the linguine until al dente.

13. Drain and transfer the linguine to the pot with the sauce. Toss over high heat for 1 minute.

14. Add the fried zucchini and fold gently for 30 seconds.

Service

Divide among 4 plates and serve immediately.

Chef's note

Eggplant and zucchini are fried separately because they absorb oil and cook at different rates. Adding the zucchini only at the end keeps its shape intact while the eggplant becomes part of the sauce.
history: A Calabrian regional preparation associated by name with Aspromonte, this pasta combines peppers, mushrooms, eggplant, zucchini, and tomato—ingredients characteristic of the region’s mountain-and-Mediterranean pantry. Standard regional references document the preparation but do not establish a single inventor or creation date.
description: Calabrian linguine with eggplant, zucchini, bell peppers, mushrooms, tomato, celery, and fresh herbs. The main ingredients remain central throughout the preparation, making the finished serving easy to visualize and the dish’s defining components immediately understandable.
