title: Calabrian Pasta and Potatoes with Egg
instructions:
Calabrian Pasta and Potatoes with Egg

Calabrian ditalini with fried new potatoes, fresh sausage, eggs, pecorino, and parsley.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

2/3 lb ditalini
4 large eggs
4 medium new potatoes
1/2 cup finely grated pecorino
2 links fresh Italian sausage
1/4 cup finely chopped fresh parsley
2 cups plus 2 tbsp olive oil for frying
3/4 tsp fine salt
1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper

For cooking the pasta
3 1/4 qt water
1 tbsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Scrub the new potatoes thoroughly in warm water without peeling them.

2. Cut the potatoes into roughly 5/8-inch cubes and dry them completely.

3. Heat the olive oil to 340°F. Fry the potatoes in batches for 6–8 minutes, until tender inside and golden outside.

4. Lift the potatoes out with a slotted spoon, season with 1/2 teaspoon salt, and reserve. Measure and reserve 1/4 cup of the frying oil; cool the rest before discarding it.

5. Beat the eggs in a bowl. Add the pecorino and parsley and whisk until evenly combined.

6. Remove the casings from the sausages and crumble the meat into a skillet. Cook over medium heat for 6–8 minutes, stirring, until completely cooked and lightly browned.

7. Bring the pasta water and salt to a boil. Cook the ditalini until 3 minutes short of the package's stated cooking time. Drain.

8. Heat the reserved 1/4 cup frying oil in a wide skillet over medium heat.

9. Add the pasta, potatoes, and sausage and toss for 1 minute.

10. Reduce the heat to low. Pour in the egg-and-pecorino mixture and add the black pepper and remaining 1/4 teaspoon salt.

11. Stir continuously for 2–3 minutes, until the eggs are just set and evenly coat the pasta and potatoes.

Service

Divide immediately among 4 plates and serve very hot.

Chef's note

Drain the pasta very al dente because it finishes cooking in the skillet. Keep the heat low once the eggs are added so they set into a soft coating rather than becoming dry.
history: A traditional Calabrian home-style pasta, this preparation combines fried new potatoes, eggs, pecorino, sausage, parsley, and black pepper with short pasta. The dialect term trimma is documented in Gerhard Rohlfs’s 1977 Nuovo Dizionario Dialettale della Calabria, confirming the name’s regional linguistic roots. Its legacy endures.
description: Crisp-edged potatoes, savory sausage, short pasta, eggs, pecorino, parsley, and black pepper come together in a rich skillet meal. Ditalini pasta carries the dish’s defining ingredients. The eggs bind everything into a hearty, deeply comforting plate with contrasting creamy and fried textures.

title: Maccheroni alla Toranese
instructions:
Maccheroni alla Toranese

Calabrian macaroni with browned pancetta, slowly stewed onions, pecorino, and ground red chile.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

7/8 lb mezzani or maltagliati
about 1/4 lb lean pancetta, diced
1/3 cup plus 1 tbsp plus 1 tsp extra-virgin olive oil
2 large onions, finely chopped
1 cup finely grated pecorino
1/2 tsp ground red chile
3/4 tsp fine salt

For cooking the pasta
4 1/4 qt water
1 tbsp plus 1/3 tsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Heat the extra-virgin olive oil in a wide pot over medium heat.

2. Add the pancetta and brown for 5–6 minutes, until well colored and some of its fat has rendered.

3. Lift out the pancetta with a slotted spoon and reserve it, leaving the oil and rendered fat in the pot.

4. Add the onions and fine salt. Reduce the heat to low and cook for 25–30 minutes, stirring every 3–4 minutes, until the onions are completely soft and nearly broken down without burning.

5. Return the pancetta to the pot and stir for 2 minutes.

6. Bring the pasta water and salt to a boil. Cook the mezzani or maltagliati until al dente.

7. Drain and transfer the pasta directly to the pot with the onions and pancetta.

8. Toss over medium heat for 1 minute.

9. Turn off the heat, add 3/4 cup of the pecorino, and toss vigorously for 30 seconds.

Service

Divide among 4 plates. Top with the remaining 1/4 cup pecorino. Serve the ground red chile at the table, dividing the measured amount among the diners according to preference.

Chef's note

Cook the onions slowly until they are almost falling apart because they form the base of the sauce. Add the pecorino off the heat so it stays creamy rather than separating or turning rubbery.
history: This Calabrian pasta comes from Torano Castello in Cosenza Province. Traditional versions combine short pasta with slowly softened onions, cured pork, pecorino, and red chile. Some recipes use lardo or guanciale; others use pancetta, reflecting household variation within the same local tradition. Its legacy endures.
description: Sweet onions cook down until almost creamy, absorbing the rendered richness of browned cured pork. Tossed with short pasta, pecorino, and red chile, the result is intensely savory, gently sweet, and remarkably full-flavored from a short ingredient list.

title: Malloreddus alla Campidanese
instructions:
Malloreddus alla Campidanese

Sardinian malloreddus with sausage ragù, tomato, saffron, and Pecorino Sardo.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

7/8 lb malloreddus
2/3 lb fresh Sardinian sausage
2 cups plus 2 tbsp tomato passata
1 medium onion, finely chopped
1 packet Sardinian saffron
1 cup finely grated Pecorino Sardo
3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
2/3 tsp fine salt
1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper
3 tbsp plus 1 tsp hot water

For cooking the pasta
4 1/4 qt water
1 tbsp plus 1 1/2 tsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Remove the sausage casings and crumble the meat by hand into small, irregular pieces.

2. Heat the olive oil in a wide skillet over medium-low heat. Add the onion and cook for 5–6 minutes, until soft and translucent.

3. Add the sausage and brown over medium heat for 6–8 minutes, breaking it apart with a wooden spoon.

4. Add the passata and fine salt. Bring to a gentle simmer, reduce the heat, and cook uncovered for 30 minutes, stirring every 5 minutes.

5. Dissolve the saffron in the hot water and stir it into the sauce during the final 5 minutes.

6. Bring the pasta water and salt to a boil. Cook the malloreddus until al dente.

7. Drain and transfer the malloreddus directly to the skillet.

8. Add 3/4 cup of the Pecorino and toss over low heat for 1 minute.

9. Turn off the heat and add the black pepper.

Service

Divide among 4 plates and finish with the remaining 1/4 cup Pecorino.

Chef's note

Add the saffron only during the final few minutes so its aroma remains distinct. Keep the sausage in small, irregular pieces rather than reducing it to a fine mince.
history: One of Sardinia’s best-known pasta traditions, these ridged semolina dumplings are especially associated with Campidano. Sardegna Turismo describes malloreddus as among the island’s oldest and most widespread pasta forms; the Campidanese version became famous for its sausage ragù.

title: Culurgiones D'ogliastra
instructions:
Culurgiones D'ogliastra

Sardinian wheat-ear-shaped dumplings filled with potato, Pecorino Sardo, mint, and garlic-infused olive oil, served with tomato sauce.

Yield: about 60 culurgiones

Ingredients

For the dough
2 1/2 cups type 00 flour
1 1/4 cups fine durum-wheat semolina
1 1/4 cups room-temperature water
1 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
3/4 tsp fine salt

For the filling
2 1/4 lb yellow-fleshed potatoes
1 cup finely grated Pecorino Sardo
6 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
1 garlic clove
14 fresh mint leaves, finely chopped
1 tsp fine salt
1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper

For the tomato sauce
2 cups plus 2 tbsp tomato passata
2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
1 garlic clove
3 fresh basil leaves
1/2 tsp fine salt

For cooking the culurgiones
6 1/3 qt water
2 tbsp plus 1 tsp fine salt

Preparation

1. At least 8 hours ahead, put the garlic clove for the filling into the olive oil. Cover and leave to infuse.

2. Boil the unpeeled potatoes in unsalted water for 30–40 minutes, until a knife passes easily through the center.

3. Drain, peel while still hot, and pass through a potato ricer. Cool completely.

4. Remove the garlic from the infused oil. Combine the potatoes with the Pecorino, mint, salt, pepper, and all of the garlic-infused oil.

5. Cover the filling and refrigerate overnight.

6. Make the dough. Combine the type 00 flour and semolina. Add the olive oil, water, and salt.

7. Knead for 10 minutes, until smooth and elastic. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.

8. Roll the dough thin, about 1/32 inch, and cut into rounds about 3 inches in diameter.

9. Put about 1 tablespoon filling in the center of each round.

10. Close each culurgione with the traditional wheat-ear seam: pinch one end, then alternate small folds from the right and left, overlapping them until the filling is completely sealed.

11. Make the sauce. Heat the olive oil in a saucepan. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute.

12. Add the passata, salt, and basil. Cook over medium-low heat for 20 minutes. Remove the garlic.

13. Bring the cooking water and salt to a boil.

14. Cook the culurgiones in batches. Once they float, continue cooking for 1 minute and lift them out with a slotted spoon.

Service

Spoon hot tomato sauce onto the plates and arrange the culurgiones over it. Serve immediately.

Chef's note

The filling should be completely cold before shaping. Resting it overnight firms the potato, Pecorino, mint, and garlic oil mixture and makes the wheat-ear closure easier to form.
history: A defining pasta of Ogliastra, these hand-sealed dumplings are traditionally filled with potato, cheese, and herbs and finished with the distinctive wheat-ear closure called sa spighitta. The Ogliastra version holds IGP status and remains closely tied to holidays and family celebrations.
description: Delicate hand-shaped pasta encloses a fragrant filling of potato, pecorino, mint, and garlic, then meets bright tomato sauce. The striking wheat-ear seal adds craft and elegance to a filling that is creamy, aromatic, and deeply rooted in Sardinian home cooking.

title: Fregola with Clams
instructions:
Fregola with Clams

Assemini-style Sardinian fregola with small clams, fresh tomato, sun-dried tomato, garlic, parsley, and chile.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

2/3 lb coarse Sardinian fregola
1 1/3 lb small clams
4 1/4 cups hot light fish stock
1 1/2 cups diced fresh sauce tomatoes
2 sun-dried tomatoes, finely chopped
2 garlic cloves
3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
1/4 cup finely chopped fresh parsley
1/4 tsp dried chile flakes

For purging the clams
2 1/8 qt cold water
3 tbsp plus 1 tsp sea salt

Preparation

1. Rinse the clams and place them in a bowl with the cold water and sea salt. Purge for 60 minutes.

2. Drain and rinse the clams again.

3. Put them in a wide pot, cover, and cook over high heat for 4–5 minutes, removing them as they open. Discard any that remain closed.

4. Strain the clam liquid carefully through a fine-mesh strainer. Remove about two-thirds of the clams from their shells and leave the remainder in the shell.

5. Combine the strained clam liquid with the hot fish stock and keep the mixture at a gentle simmer.

6. Heat the olive oil in a wide saucepan. Add the garlic and sun-dried tomatoes and cook for 1 minute.

7. Add the fresh tomatoes and cook for 5 minutes.

8. Add the fregola and toast it in the sauce for 1 minute.

9. Add the hot stock one ladle at a time, stirring regularly. Cook for about 12 minutes, keeping the fregola loose and semi-brothy throughout.

10. During the final 2 minutes, add both the shelled clams and those left in their shells.

11. Turn off the heat and add the parsley and chile.

Service

Divide among 4 bowls and serve immediately with a consistency closer to a thick soup than a dry risotto.

Chef's note

The strained clam liquid belongs in the cooking broth because it carries much of the seafood flavor. Traditional fregola with clams should remain deliberately loose rather than cooking down completely dry.
history: Fregola is a traditional Sardinian toasted semolina pasta, long associated with the island’s coastal and inland cooking. Pairing it with arselle—small clams—became one of its most recognizable preparations, marrying the pasta’s nutty toasted character with concentrated shellfish broth.
description: Toasted semolina pearls simmer directly in briny clam liquor with tomato, garlic, and chile, absorbing the sea into every bite. The texture stays pleasantly chewy while the broth turns silky and savory, creating a comforting coastal bowl with remarkable depth.

title: Lorighittas with Rooster Ragù
instructions:
Lorighittas with Rooster Ragù

Sardinian lorighittas with slow-cooked rooster, tomato, red wine, bay leaf, and Pecorino Sardo.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

13/16 lb lorighittas
1 small rooster, about 2 1/4–2 2/3 lb, cleaned and cut into pieces
3 cups tomato passata
1 medium yellow onion, finely chopped
1 garlic clove
4 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
1/3 cup plus 1 tbsp dry red wine
2/3 cup hot water or unsalted light broth
1 bay leaf
3 fresh basil leaves
1 tsp fine salt
1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper
2/3 cup finely grated Pecorino Sardo

For cooking the pasta
4 1/4 qt water
1 tbsp plus 1 1/2 tsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Pat the rooster pieces thoroughly dry.

2. Heat the olive oil in a wide pot and brown the rooster for 8–10 minutes, turning until colored on all sides.

3. Add the onion and garlic and cook for 5 minutes.

4. Pour in the red wine and cook for 2–3 minutes, until the sharp alcohol aroma has largely cooked away.

5. Add the passata, bay leaf, 1/2 cup of the hot water or broth, salt, and pepper. Cover with the lid slightly ajar.

6. Cook over low heat for 60–75 minutes, turning the pieces every 15 minutes. If the sauce reduces too far, add the remaining liquid.

7. Remove the rooster from the sauce. Debone and shred about 1/2 lb of the meat and return it to the pot. Keep the remaining rooster warm for serving.

8. Add the basil and cook the sauce for another 5 minutes.

9. Bring the pasta water and salt to a boil. Cook the lorighittas until al dente, reserving 2/3 cup pasta water.

10. Drain and transfer the pasta to the ragù. Add 1/4 cup pasta water and toss for 1–2 minutes.

11. Turn off the heat and fold in about 1/2 cup Pecorino.

Service

Divide among 4 plates and finish with the remaining Pecorino. Serve the remaining rooster pieces separately or alongside the pasta.

Chef's note

Cook the rooster slowly until tender without drying it out. Shredding part of the meat into the sauce helps the ragù cling to the lorighittas, while the remaining pieces can be served as a second course.
history: Lorighittas are a hand-braided pasta unique to Morgongiori in western Sardinia, with written documentation dating to the 16th century. Traditionally made for special occasions, especially All Saints’ Day, they are often served with a slow sauce of cockerel, pork, or wild boar. Its legacy endures.
description: Intricately braided pasta holds a slow-cooked rooster ragù enriched with tomato, red wine, bay, and pecorino. The twisted rings stay wonderfully chewy while trapping the concentrated sauce, delivering a festive, deeply savory plate with rustic elegance.

ingredients:
For the maccarrones

title: Maccarrones de Busa
instructions:
Maccarrones de Busa

Sardinian hand-shaped pasta formed around a busa, served with tomato, basil, and Pecorino Sardo.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

For the maccarrones
2 1/2 cups fine durum-wheat semolina
3/4 cup plus 2 tbsp plus 2 tsp warm water
2/3 tsp fine salt

For the sauce
2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
1 garlic clove
3 cups tomato passata
5 fresh basil leaves
2/3 tsp fine salt
3/4 cup finely grated Pecorino Sardo

For cooking the pasta
3 1/4 qt water
1 tbsp plus 1 tsp fine salt
1/3 cup plus 1 tbsp pasta cooking water to reserve

Preparation

1. Mound the semolina on the work surface and form a well.

2. Dissolve the salt in the warm water. Add the water gradually to the semolina and knead for 8–10 minutes, until smooth and elastic.

3. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.

4. Make the sauce. Heat the olive oil in a saucepan, add the garlic, and cook for 2 minutes without burning it.

5. Add the passata and fine salt. Cook over medium-low heat for 25 minutes.

6. Add the basil during the final 5 minutes. Remove the garlic.

7. Roll the dough into ropes about 3/8 inch thick and cut into pieces 2–2 1/2 inches long.

8. Wrap each piece around a busa, thin metal rod, or metal skewer. Roll gently to thin and lengthen it, then slide the pasta off.

9. Arrange the maccarrones on a semolina-dusted tray and dry for 30 minutes.

10. Bring the pasta water and salt to a boil. Cook the maccarrones for 5–7 minutes. Before draining, reserve the measured pasta water.

11. Transfer the pasta to a skillet with about three-quarters of the sauce. Add 3 tablespoons plus 1 teaspoon pasta water and toss for 1–2 minutes.

12. Turn off the heat and fold in 1/2 cup Pecorino.

Service

Divide among 4 plates. Finish with the remaining sauce and remaining Pecorino.

Chef's note

The busa creates the characteristic central hole that allows sauce to enter the pasta. A short drying period after shaping helps the maccarrones retain their form during boiling.
history: A traditional Sardinian fresh pasta, especially associated with Barbagia and Nuoro, these long hollow strands are shaped by wrapping dough around a thin iron rod called a busa. The technique reflects the island’s hand-made pasta culture passed through generations. Its place at the table endures.
description: Sardinian hand-shaped pasta formed around a busa, served with tomato, basil, and Pecorino Sardo.

title: Maccarrones a Bocciu
instructions:
Maccarrones a Bocciu

Sardinian grater-shaped dumplings with sausage-tomato sauce, semi-aged Pecorino Canestrino, and fresh herbs.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

For the dough
2 1/2 cups type 00 flour
1 7/8 cups fine durum-wheat semolina
3 large eggs
1/3 cup plus 1 tbsp warm water
3 tbsp softened butter
3/4 tsp fine salt

For the sauce
1 1/4 cups crushed peeled tomatoes
scant 1/2 lb Sardinian pork sausage
1 1/2 cups finely grated semi-aged Pecorino Canestrino

2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
1/4 cup finely chopped fresh parsley
8 fresh basil leaves
2/3 tsp fine salt

For cooking the pasta
4 1/4 qt water
1 tbsp plus 1 1/2 tsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Combine the type 00 flour and semolina on the work surface and form a well.

2. Beat the eggs with the salt and warm water.

3. Pour the mixture into the well and gradually incorporate the flours.

4. Add the softened butter and knead for 10 minutes, until the dough is smooth and firm.

5. Cover with a kitchen towel and rest in a cool place for 30 minutes.

6. Make the sauce. Heat the olive oil in a saucepan and add the onion. Cook over medium-low heat for 5 minutes.

7. Remove the sausage casing, crumble the meat, and add it to the onion. Brown for 6 minutes.

8. Add the crushed tomatoes, salt, basil, and half of the parsley. Cook over low heat for 25 minutes.

9. Roll the dough into ropes and cut into pieces about 3/4 inch long.

10. Press each piece with your thumb against the inside surface of a grater, dragging slightly to create a hollow, rough dumpling.

11. Bring the pasta water and salt to a boil. Cook the maccarrones until al dente, about 4–6 minutes.

12. Drain and transfer directly to the sauce. Toss for 1 minute.

13. Turn off the heat and add 1 cup Pecorino and the remaining parsley.

Service

Divide among 4 plates and finish with the remaining 1/2 cup Pecorino.

Chef's note

The rough grater-marked surface is what holds the sauce. Add the Pecorino off the heat so it melts into the sauce without separating.
history: This lesser-known Sardinian handmade pasta belongs to the island’s broad tradition of shaping semolina dough by hand on simple household tools. Its precise origin is less documented than other Sardinian forms, but it reflects the same rural, resourceful pasta culture preserved across the island.
description: Rustic handmade pasta with a rough, sauce-catching surface meets a savory sausage-and-tomato dressing finished with pecorino. The texture is hearty and satisfying, while the sauce brings deep pork flavor, gentle sweetness, and the warmth of traditional Sardinian cooking.

title: Linguine with Sea Urchin
instructions:
Linguine with Sea Urchin

Linguine with fresh sea-urchin roe, tomato, garlic, butter, and extra-virgin olive oil.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

3/4 lb linguine
22 very fresh edible sea urchins
2 cups plus 2 tbsp tomato pulp
1 garlic clove
2 tbsp unsalted butter
2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
1/2 tsp fine salt
1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper

For cooking the pasta
4 1/4 qt water
1 tbsp plus 1/3 tsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Wear sturdy gloves. Hold each sea urchin in a thick kitchen towel and cut it open carefully with strong kitchen scissors.

2. Discard the dark liquid and innards. With a small spoon, remove only the five orange roe lobes from each urchin and place them in a chilled bowl. Refrigerate until the final step.

3. Heat the butter and olive oil in a wide skillet over medium-low heat.

4. Add the whole garlic clove and cook for 1–2 minutes, until golden. Remove it.

5. Add the tomato pulp, fine salt, and black pepper. Cook over low heat for 15 minutes.

6. Bring the pasta water and salt to a boil. Cook the linguine until 2 minutes short of the package's stated cooking time.

7. Drain and transfer the pasta to the tomato sauce. Toss over medium heat for 2 minutes.

8. Turn off the heat completely. Add the sea-urchin roe and fold gently for 30 seconds using only the residual heat.

Service

Divide immediately among 4 plates and serve hot.

Chef's note

Do not boil the sea-urchin roe. Adding it off the heat protects its delicate marine aroma and creamy texture. Use only sea urchins sold for food by an authorized source and keep them well chilled until opening.
history: Sea urchin pasta belongs to the coastal cooking of Sardinia and other Mediterranean regions, where fresh ricci are prized for their intense briny roe. The preparation is traditionally kept simple so the roe’s marine sweetness remains the central flavor. Its place at the table endures.
description: Silky linguine is coated with the vivid, oceanic richness of fresh sea urchin, balanced by garlic, olive oil, and tomato. Luxurious yet elemental, it tastes intensely of the sea and delivers a creamy texture without relying on heavy sauce.

title: Spaghetti with Mullet Bottarga
instructions:
Spaghetti with Mullet Bottarga

Sardinian spaghetti with grated mullet bottarga, garlic, parsley, lemon zest, extra-virgin olive oil, and chile.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

about 3/4 lb spaghetti

finely grated zest of 1 unwaxed lemon
1/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil, divided

For cooking the pasta
3 3/4 qt water
1 tbsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Bring the pasta water and salt to a boil.

2. Heat 3 tablespoons olive oil in a wide skillet over low heat.

3. Add the garlic and chile. Cook for 2 minutes, until the garlic is just golden.

4. Add 1/4 cup pasta water and remove the garlic.

5. Cook the spaghetti until 3 minutes short of the package's stated cooking time.

6. Drain, reserving another 1/2 cup pasta water, and transfer the spaghetti to the skillet.

7. Finish cooking for 3 minutes over medium-high heat, adding the reserved pasta water in three additions and tossing continuously to create a glossy emulsion.

8. Turn off the heat completely.

9. Add the parsley, lemon zest, and 8 tablespoons bottarga. Toss vigorously for 30 seconds.

10. Add the remaining 1 tablespoon olive oil and toss again.

Service

Divide among 4 plates and finish each serving with 1/2 tablespoon of the remaining bottarga.

Chef's note

Add the bottarga only after the heat is turned off. Residual heat is enough to distribute its flavor without cooking it, while the starchy pasta water creates the emulsion without requiring excessive oil.
history: Bottarga has ancient Mediterranean roots and has long been important in Sardinia, especially around Cabras and other lagoon and coastal communities. Grey-mullet roe is salted and dried into the amber delicacy often called ‘Sardinian caviar,’ then shaved or grated over pasta.

title: Zuppa Gallurese
instructions:
Zuppa Gallurese

Gallura-style baked bread casserole with pane carasau, meat broth, and generous layers of Pecorino Sardo.

Yield: 6–8 servings

Ingredients

For the broth
1 1/3 lb sheep meat or beef suitable for broth
8 1/2 cups cold water
1 onion
2 garlic cloves
1/2 cup fresh parsley leaves
10 fresh basil leaves
1 1/3 tsp fine salt

For the casserole
1 1/8 lb pane carasau
4 cups thinly sliced mild Pecorino Sardo
3 cups finely grated aged Pecorino Sardo
1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper
2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil

Preparation

1. Put the meat in a large pot with the cold water, quartered onion, garlic, parsley, and basil.

2. Bring slowly to a boil, skim away any foam, and reduce the heat.

3. Simmer gently for about 2 hours.

4. Add the fine salt during the final 20 minutes.

5. Strain through a fine sieve. Measure 6 1/3 cups hot broth for the casserole; reserve the meat for another use.

6. Preheat the oven to 350°F.

7. Grease a deep baking dish with 1 tablespoon olive oil.

8. Arrange a layer of pane carasau and moisten it evenly with hot broth without turning it to mush.

9. Cover with portions of the mild Pecorino, aged Pecorino, and a small amount of black pepper.

10. Repeat the layers until the bread and cheeses are used, finishing with aged Pecorino.

11. Slowly pour the remaining broth around the edges and into several points in the dish so every layer is moistened.

12. Drizzle the remaining 1 tablespoon olive oil over the top.

13. Bake at 350°F for 25 minutes, until the cheese is fully melted and the surface is golden.

14. Rest for 10 minutes.

Service

Cut into 6–8 portions and serve very hot.

Chef's note

The bread should absorb the broth without dissolving completely. Adding the liquid gradually throughout the layers keeps the finished casserole soft while preserving its structure.
history: A signature dish of Gallura in northern Sardinia, suppa cuata layers stale bread, broth, and cheese. Its exact origin is uncertain. The name means ‘hidden soup’ and is often linked to an old method of cooking the covered pan beneath hot embers. Its legacy endures.
description: Stale bread becomes luxuriously tender as it absorbs rich meat broth beneath layers of melted cheese and herbs. Baked until deeply savory and cohesive, it transforms humble ingredients into a warming, celebratory casserole with remarkable depth and comfort.

title: Pane Frattau
instructions:
Pane Frattau

Sardinian pane carasau softened in broth and layered with tomato sauce, Pecorino Sardo, and a poached egg.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

For the pane frattau
8 sheets pane carasau
1 1/2 cups tomato passata
5 cups lamb or sheep broth
1/2 onion, finely chopped
1 1/2 cups finely grated Pecorino Sardo
2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
12 fresh basil leaves
3/4 tsp fine salt

For the poached eggs
4 large eggs
2 1/8 qt water
3/4 cup plus 1 tbsp plus 1 tsp white wine vinegar
3/4 tsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Heat the olive oil in a small saucepan over medium-low heat. Add the onion and cook for 5 minutes, until soft.

2. Add the passata and 1/2 teaspoon salt. Cook over medium heat for 14 minutes.

3. Add 8 basil leaves during the final 2 minutes. Turn off the heat.

4. Heat the lamb or sheep broth in a wide pot and keep it just below a boil.

5. For the poached eggs, bring the water to a gentle simmer with the vinegar and remaining 1/4 teaspoon salt.

6. Crack one egg into a small bowl. Create a gentle vortex in the water and slide the egg into the center.

7. Cook for 2 minutes, until the white is set and the yolk remains soft. Lift out with a slotted spoon and blot on paper towels. Repeat with the remaining eggs.

8. Break each sheet of pane carasau into 4 pieces.

9. Dip each piece into the hot broth for 2–3 seconds, only long enough to soften it.

10. Assemble four plates. On each plate, arrange 4 pieces of bread, a portion of tomato sauce, and 2 tablespoons Pecorino.

11. Repeat to create a second matching layer.

12. Finish each plate with the remaining Pecorino, one poached egg, and one basil leaf.

Service

Serve immediately while the bread, sauce, and broth are hot and the egg yolk remains soft.

Chef's note

Dip the pane carasau for only a few seconds so it becomes flexible without falling apart. Poach the eggs last and serve at once so the yolks remain fluid.
history: A frugal Sardinian dish rooted in pastoral life, it developed as a way to use broken pieces of pane carasau carried by shepherds. The bread is softened, layered with tomato and pecorino, and topped with a poached egg, turning leftovers into a complete meal.
description: Crisp flatbread softens in hot broth, then layers with tomato, pecorino, and a runny poached egg. The yolk becomes a rich sauce, bringing together salty cheese, bright tomato, and tender bread in a simple but deeply satisfying plate.

title: Spaghetti alla Carbonara
instructions:
Spaghetti alla Carbonara

Roman carbonara with spaghetti, guanciale, egg yolks, whole egg, Pecorino Romano, and black pepper.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

3/4 lb spaghetti
1/4 lb guanciale, diced or cut into strips
4 large egg yolks
1 large egg
1 cup finely grated Pecorino Romano, plus a little extra for serving
1 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil or 1 tbsp lard
1 tsp freshly ground black pepper
1/2 cup reserved pasta cooking water, plus more only if required

For cooking the pasta
4 qt water
1 tbsp salt

Preparation

1. Bring the water to a boil and add the salt.

2. Heat the olive oil or lard in a wide skillet over medium-low heat. Add the guanciale and cook for 6–8 minutes, until its fat turns translucent and the edges become crisp without drying out the lean portion. Reduce the heat to very low.

3. In a large bowl, whisk the egg yolks and whole egg until uniform.

4. Whisk in about 3/4 cup of the Pecorino and 3/4 teaspoon of the black pepper to form a thick cream.

5. Cook the spaghetti until al dente. Before draining, reserve at least 1/2 cup pasta water.

6. Transfer the spaghetti to the skillet with the guanciale and toss for 30 seconds to coat it with the rendered fat.

7. Remove the skillet completely from the heat.

8. Slowly whisk the 1/2 cup hot pasta water into the egg-and-cheese mixture.

9. Immediately pour the mixture over the spaghetti off the heat and toss rapidly with tongs or two forks for 30–60 seconds. If the sauce is too thick, add additional pasta water 1 tablespoon at a time.

10. The finished sauce should be glossy and creamy with no visible scrambled egg.

Service

Divide among 4 warm plates. Finish with the remaining 1/4 cup Pecorino and remaining 1/4 teaspoon black pepper.

Chef's note

Add the egg mixture only after the pan is off the heat. The heat retained by the pasta and cooking water should thicken the sauce without scrambling the eggs.
history: Now a symbol of Roman cooking, carbonara is surprisingly modern and its exact origin remains debated. Italian printed versions appeared in the 1950s, evolving toward today’s combination of pasta, guanciale, eggs, pecorino, and black pepper. Its regional identity remains firmly rooted in the local table today.
description: Crisp guanciale, silky eggs, sharp Pecorino Romano, and black pepper form a glossy sauce that clings to hot spaghetti without cream. Rich, salty, peppery, and intensely satisfying, it is Roman comfort food at its most concentrated.

title: Bucatini All'amatriciana
instructions:
Bucatini All'amatriciana

Bucatini all'Amatriciana with guanciale, San Marzano tomatoes, Pecorino di Amatrice, and fresh red chile.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

3/4 lb bucatini
1 3/4 cups chopped ripe San Marzano tomatoes
scant 1/4 lb guanciale, cut into narrow batons
3/4 cup finely grated Pecorino di Amatrice
1 small fresh red chile, sliced
1 tsp extra-virgin olive oil
1/2 tsp fine salt for the sauce

For cooking the pasta
4 1/4 qt water
1 tbsp plus 1 tsp salt

Preparation

1. Cut a shallow X in the base of each tomato.

2. Bring a small pot of water to a boil. Blanch the tomatoes for 1 minute, then immediately transfer them to ice water.

3. Peel the tomatoes, remove the hard cores and seeds, and chop the flesh.

4. Heat the olive oil in a wide saucepan. Add the guanciale and cook over medium-low heat for 5–6 minutes, until golden and the fat has rendered.

5. Remove the guanciale with a slotted spoon and reserve it.

6. Add the chile and tomatoes to the saucepan containing the rendered guanciale fat. Add the fine salt.

7. Cook over medium-low heat for 30–40 minutes, stirring every 5 minutes, until thick but still fluid.

8. Return the guanciale to the sauce for the final 3 minutes.

9. Bring the pasta water and salt to a boil. Cook the bucatini until al dente.

10. Drain and transfer directly to the saucepan. Toss with the sauce for 1 minute.

11. Turn off the heat and add about 1/2 cup Pecorino. Toss until evenly distributed.

Service

Divide among 4 plates and finish with the remaining 1/4 cup Pecorino.

Chef's note

Removing the guanciale after browning and returning it only at the end preserves its texture instead of allowing it to soften during the long tomato simmer.
history: Born in Amatrice, this Lazio classic evolved from the older tomato-free gricia after tomatoes entered Italian cooking. Shepherding and transhumance helped spread the dish toward Rome, where bucatini, guanciale, tomato, chile, and pecorino became an iconic combination. Its regional identity remains firmly present at the table.
description: Smoky-crisp guanciale and bright tomato coat thick hollow bucatini, finished with salty pecorino and a touch of chile. The sauce is robust but balanced—rich pork, acidity, heat, and cheese meeting in every satisfying forkful.

title: Spaghetti Cacio e Pepe
instructions:
Spaghetti Cacio e Pepe

Roman spaghettoni with Pecorino Romano and toasted black pepper.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

2 cups finely grated medium-aged Pecorino Romano
2 tsp whole black peppercorns

For cooking the pasta
2 2/3 qt water
2 tsp salt

Preparation

1. Bring the water to a boil and add the salt.

2. Finely grate all of the Pecorino and reserve 3 tbsp for serving.

3. Coarsely crush the peppercorns.

4. Heat a wide skillet over low heat. Add the pepper and toast for 2 minutes, moving the skillet continuously.

5. Add 1/2 cup pasta water to the toasted pepper and keep the skillet over low heat.

6. Cook the spaghettoni until 3 minutes short of the package's stated cooking time.

7. Reserve another 1 cup pasta water and drain the pasta.

8. Transfer the spaghettoni to the skillet with the pepper. Finish cooking for 2–3 minutes, adding 1/2 cup of the reserved water and stirring continuously.

9. Put the remaining 1 3/4 cups Pecorino in a bowl. Add the final 1/2 cup hot pasta water in 3 equal additions, whisking until smooth.

10. When the pasta is cooked, remove the skillet completely from the heat and wait 30 seconds.

11. Add the Pecorino cream and toss vigorously with tongs for 60–90 seconds, until creamy and uniform.

Serving

Divide among 4 plates and finish with the reserved Pecorino and the pepper remaining in the skillet.

Chef's Note

Do not expose the Pecorino to direct heat during the final toss. Removing the pan from the burner helps prevent the cheese proteins from tightening into clumps.
history: A cornerstone of Roman pasta cooking, this dish reflects Lazio’s pastoral traditions and reliance on durable ingredients carried by shepherds: dried pasta, aged pecorino, and black pepper. Its power comes from technique rather than a long ingredient list.

instructions:
Rigatoni with Pajata

Roman rigatoni with butcher-prepared veal pajata, slow tomato sauce, soffritto, white wine, and Pecorino Romano.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

1 3/4 lb butcher-prepared and cleaned milk-fed veal pajata

For cooking the pasta

Preparation

1. Use pajata already prepared by a qualified butcher and keep it refrigerated until cooking.

2. Cut the pajata into lengths 8–10 inches long. Form each piece into a ring and tie the ends with kitchen twine.

3. Melt the lard in a heavy pot over medium-low heat.

4. Add the onion, carrot, and celery and cook for 8 minutes.

5. Add the pajata and brown gently for 8–10 minutes, turning the rings without breaking them.

6. Pour in the white wine and cook for 3 minutes.

7. Add the passata, whole clove, fine salt, and pepper.

8. Bring to a gentle simmer, cover with the lid slightly ajar, and cook over low heat for 2 hours. Turn the pajata gently every 25 minutes.

9. Remove the whole clove.

10. Bring the pasta water and salt to a boil. Cook the rigatoni al dente.

11. Drain the rigatoni and transfer to a wide skillet with 2 cups pajata sauce. Toss for 1 minute.

12. Turn off the heat and fold in 1/2 cup Pecorino.

Serving

Divide the rigatoni among 4 plates. Distribute the pajata rings and remaining sauce evenly among the 4 portions, then finish each plate with 1 tablespoon of the remaining Pecorino.

Chef's Note

Handle the pajata gently throughout cooking so the rings do not break. The long, low simmer tenderizes the pajata while concentrating the tomato sauce gradually.
history: A classic of Rome’s quinto quarto tradition, this dish is strongly associated with Testaccio, once home to the city slaughterhouse. Workers used inexpensive offal such as calf intestine, turning humble cuts into one of Roman trattoria cooking’s most distinctive specialties.
description: Tender rings of milk-fed calf intestine braise in tomato until creamy inside, then coat sturdy rigatoni with pecorino and pepper. Rich, earthy, and deeply Roman, it turns a humble butcher’s cut into an unusually luxurious pasta sauce.

instructions:
Rigatoni alla Gricia

Pasta alla Gricia with crisp guanciale, Pecorino Romano, and black pepper.

Yield: 6 servings

Ingredients

1 1/8 lb rigatoni or spaghettoni
scant 1/2 lb guanciale, cut into strips
1 1/2 cups finely grated Pecorino Romano
1 1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper
1/2 cup reserved pasta cooking water

For cooking the pasta
5 1/4 qt water
1 tbsp plus 1/3 tsp salt

Preparation

1. Bring the water and salt to a boil.

2. Put the guanciale in a large cold skillet.

3. Set over medium-low heat and cook for 6–8 minutes, stirring, until the fat turns translucent and the guanciale is golden and lightly crisp.

4. Turn off the heat and leave the guanciale in its rendered fat.

5. Cook the pasta until al dente. Before draining, reserve 1/2 cup cooking water.

6. Transfer the pasta directly to the skillet with the guanciale and fat.

7. Return the skillet to medium heat and add 1/2 cup pasta water. Toss for 1 minute to begin forming an emulsion.

8. Remove the skillet completely from the heat.

9. Add 1 cup Pecorino gradually, tossing vigorously for 30 seconds.

10. Add 1 teaspoon black pepper and continue tossing until creamy.

Service

Divide among 6 plates and finish with the remaining 1/2 cup Pecorino and remaining 1/2 teaspoon black pepper.

Chef's note

No additional cooking fat is needed. Starting the guanciale in a cold skillet allows it to render the fat that forms the base of the sauce. Add the Pecorino off the heat to prevent clumping.
history: Rigatoni alla Gricia is rooted in the cooking of Rieti in Lazio, defined by pasta alla Gricia with crisp guanciale. Without a documented inventor or founding date, its history survives through the ingredients and technique themselves, keeping the preparation connected to the table traditions of Lazio.
description: Crisp guanciale, melted pork fat, sharp pecorino, and black pepper cling to hot rigatoni in a sauce with no tomato and nowhere to hide. Deeply savory, salty, and peppery, it is elemental Roman cooking built on flawless technique.

title: Fettuccine alla Papalina
instructions:
Fettuccine alla Papalina

Roman egg fettuccine with prosciutto, peas, onion, butter, egg yolks, and Parmigiano.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

about 3/4 lb egg fettuccine
scant 1/4 lb mild prosciutto, cut into thin strips
1 small white onion, finely chopped
3 tbsp butter
2 egg yolks
1/3 cup plus 1 tbsp finely grated Parmigiano Reggiano
2/3 cup peas, fresh or frozen
1 tsp freshly ground black pepper
1/2 cup reserved pasta cooking water

For cooking the pasta
3 3/4 qt water
1 tbsp plus 1/3 tsp salt

Preparation

1. Bring the pasta water and salt to a boil.

2. Melt the butter in a large skillet over low heat.

3. Add the onion and cook gently for 5–6 minutes, until soft and translucent.

4. Add the peas and cook over medium heat for 5–6 minutes.

5. Add the prosciutto and cook for 2 minutes, only long enough to warm and perfume the mixture without drying it out.

6. In a bowl, whisk the egg yolks with about 1/4 cup plus 2 teaspoons Parmigiano and 3/4 teaspoon black pepper.

7. Cook the fettuccine until al dente. Before draining, reserve 1/2 cup pasta water.

8. Transfer the fettuccine to the skillet with the prosciutto and peas and toss for 30 seconds.

9. Remove the skillet completely from the heat.

10. Whisk 2 tablespoons hot pasta water into the egg-yolk mixture.

11. Pour the mixture over the pasta and toss rapidly. Add additional pasta water 1 tablespoon at a time only if the sauce is too thick.

Service

Divide among 4 plates and finish with the remaining Parmigiano and remaining 1/4 teaspoon black pepper.

Chef's note

The prosciutto should only warm through; prolonged cooking makes it dry and excessively salty. Add the egg-yolk cream off the heat.
history: This Roman pasta was created in the first half of the 20th century in honor of Pope Pius XII. Tradition holds that he requested a more refined variation on familiar Roman flavors, leading to fettuccine enriched with prosciutto, peas, eggs, cheese, and butter.
description: Tender egg fettuccine is wrapped in a silky sauce of yolks, Parmigiano, butter, peas, and delicate prosciutto. Richer and gentler than carbonara, it balances sweet peas, savory ham, and creamy egg in an elegant Roman-style plate.

title: Gnocchi alla Romana
instructions:
Gnocchi alla Romana

Roman semolina rounds with milk, butter, egg yolks, grated cheese, and nutmeg, baked until golden.

Yield: 6 servings

Ingredients

4 1/4 cups whole milk
2 1/8 cups water
1 1/2 cups semolina
1/2 cup plus 1 1/2 tsp butter, divided
3/4 cup finely grated Grana Padano or Parmigiano Reggiano
2 egg yolks
1/4 tsp freshly grated nutmeg
1 tsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Pour the milk and water into a large saucepan.

2. Add 1 1/2 tablespoons of the butter and the salt. Bring almost to a boil.

3. Pour in the semolina in a steady stream while whisking continuously to prevent lumps.

4. Reduce the heat and cook for about 15 minutes, switching from the whisk to a wooden spoon as the mixture thickens.

5. Turn off the heat. Add the nutmeg, egg yolks, and about 3 tablespoons of the grated cheese, mixing vigorously after each addition.

6. Lightly wet a tray and spread the semolina mixture over it.

7. Level to an even thickness of about 5/8–3/4 inch and cool completely.

8. Cut into rounds about 2 inches in diameter.

9. Melt about 5 1/2 tablespoons butter. Use the remaining butter to grease a baking dish.

10. Arrange the rounds in the dish with their edges slightly overlapping.

11. Scatter the remaining cheese over the top and drizzle evenly with the melted butter.

12. Bake in a preheated 400°F oven for 15 minutes.

13. Switch to broil and brown for another 5 minutes, until the surface is golden.

Service

Serve immediately, allowing about 4–5 rounds per portion.

Chef's note

Cook the semolina until very thick before spreading it. Cooling it completely allows clean rounds to be cut and helps them hold their shape during browning.
history: Rome has long embraced two distinct gnocchi traditions; this version uses semolina cooked in milk, shaped into discs, and baked with butter and cheese. It became a familiar Roman home and trattoria dish, especially associated with the city’s traditional weekly meal rhythm. Its legacy endures.
description: Golden-edged semolina rounds bake beneath butter and aged cheese until crisp on top and creamy within. Nutmeg and milk add warmth and softness, creating a comforting baked dish that feels halfway between pasta, polenta, and gratin.

title: Pasta alla Zozzona
instructions:
Pasta alla Zozzona

Roman rigatoni with guanciale, pork sausage, tomatoes, egg yolks, and Pecorino Romano.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

about 3/4 lb rigatoni
scant 1/2 lb guanciale, cut into strips
9/16 lb pork sausage
2 cups canned cherry tomatoes
1 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
4 egg yolks
1 cup finely grated Pecorino Romano, divided
1/2 cup reserved pasta cooking water

For cooking the pasta
3 3/4 qt water
1 tbsp salt

Preparation

1. Bring the pasta water and salt to a boil.

2. Remove the sausage casing and break the meat into small pieces.

3. Heat the olive oil in a wide pot over medium-low heat.

4. Add the sausage and guanciale and brown for about 15 minutes, stirring regularly, until well colored.

5. Add the tomatoes, crushing them lightly with a spoon. Cover and cook for 10 minutes.

6. In a bowl, mix the egg yolks with about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons Pecorino to form a thick cream.

7. Cook the rigatoni until al dente. Before draining, reserve 1/2 cup pasta water.

8. Whisk 1/4 cup hot pasta water into the egg-and-Pecorino cream.

9. Drain the rigatoni and add them to the pot with the guanciale, sausage, and tomato. Toss for 1 minute.

10. Remove the pot completely from the heat.

11. Add the egg-and-Pecorino cream and toss rapidly for 30 seconds. Gradually add the remaining 1/4 cup pasta water over the next 30 seconds while tossing continuously.

12. Fold in the remaining Pecorino.

Service

Divide among 4 plates and serve immediately.

Chef's note

Add the egg-yolk cream only after the pot is off the heat. The rendered meat fat, tomato, starchy water, and Pecorino should emulsify without directly cooking the yolks.
history: A relatively recent Roman creation, this exuberant pasta has circulated since roughly the 1960s. It deliberately combines elements of carbonara, amatriciana, and cacio e pepe—guanciale, sausage, tomato, egg yolk, and pecorino—into one intentionally excessive sauce. Its regional identity remains firmly present at the table.
description: Roman rigatoni with guanciale, pork sausage, tomatoes, egg yolks, and Pecorino Romano.

title: Fettuccine with Chicken Giblet Ragù
instructions:
Fettuccine with Chicken Giblet Ragù

Traditional Tuscia fettuccine with chicken-giblet ragù, tomato, white wine, braised-meat sauce, and Parmigiano.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

For the fettuccine
2 1/2 cups durum-wheat semolina
4 large eggs

For the giblet ragù
1 lb mixed chicken giblets, including livers, hearts, and gizzards; where available, the traditional Viterbo version may also include food-safe combs and other poultry trim
3 1/2 tbsp finely chopped prosciutto fat
1/3 cup plus 1 tbsp olive oil
1 small onion, finely chopped
1 small carrot, finely chopped
1 celery stalk, finely chopped
1 garlic clove, minced
3/4 cup plus 1 tbsp dry white wine
1 2/3 cups crushed peeled tomatoes
1 cup braised-meat sauce
3/4 cup plus 1 tbsp water
3/4 cup finely grated Parmigiano Reggiano
3/4 tsp fine salt
1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper

For cooking the pasta
4 1/4 qt water
1 tbsp plus 1 tsp salt

Preparation

1. Clean the giblets carefully. Remove membranes, excess fat, and any green-stained portion from the livers. Open and clean the gizzards, then rinse everything briefly and pat dry.

2. If using traditional combs or other poultry trim, obtain them already prepared for food use from a qualified supplier. Blanch and peel combs before adding them to the ragù.

3. Make the fettuccine. Mound the semolina on the work surface, form a well, and add the eggs. Knead for 10 minutes until smooth. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.

4. Roll the dough to about 1/32 inch thick and cut into fettuccine 1/4–5/16 inch wide. Dust lightly with semolina and reserve.

5. Heat the olive oil in a wide pot. Add the onion, carrot, celery, garlic, and prosciutto fat. Cook over medium-low heat for 8 minutes.

6. When the prosciutto fat has rendered, add the gizzards and hearts first and brown for 5 minutes.

7. Add the livers and any other prepared giblets and cook for another 3 minutes.

8. Pour in the white wine and cook for 4 minutes, until the sharp alcohol aroma has largely cooked away.

9. Add the tomatoes, braised-meat sauce, water, fine salt, and pepper. Bring to a gentle simmer.

10. Reduce the heat and cook for 45–50 minutes, until the giblets are tender and the sauce is deeply flavored.

11. Bring the pasta water and salt to a boil. Cook the fresh fettuccine for 2–3 minutes.

12. Drain and dress immediately with the giblet ragù.

13. Add about 1/2 cup Parmigiano and toss.

Service

Divide among 4 plates and finish with the remaining Parmigiano.

Chef's note

Hearts and gizzards take longer to tenderize than livers, so they go into the pan first. Any less-common traditional poultry parts should come only from a qualified food supplier and be properly prepared before cooking.
history: An old Lazio and Roman country preparation, fettuccine with chicken giblets grew from cucina povera and whole-animal cooking. In Viterbo it was traditionally served for Easter, Ferragosto, and later Sunday lunch, while similar versions remained important around Rome and the Castelli Romani. Its legacy endures.
description: Fresh egg fettuccine is dressed with a slow, intensely savory sauce of chicken livers, hearts, vegetables, wine, tomato, and aged cheese. Earthy, rich, and deeply aromatic, it turns humble poultry parts into a luxurious Sunday-style pasta.

title: Timballo alla Bonifacio Viii
instructions:
Timballo alla Bonifacio Viii

Anagni-style timballo of fresh egg fettuccine, chicken-giblet and veal-meatball ragù, dried mushrooms, and a prosciutto casing.

Yield: 6 servings

Ingredients

1 1/2 lb firm fresh egg fettuccine
4 chicken gizzards, simmered and cut into small pieces
about 1/2 lb mixed chicken giblets, mainly livers and hearts, cleaned and coarsely chopped
4 tbsp plus 1 tsp butter, divided
2/3 lb ground veal
2 large eggs
1 cup finely grated Parmigiano Reggiano, divided
2/3 tsp fine salt
1 cup chopped peeled tomatoes
2 loosely packed cups dried porcini mushrooms
2 cups plus 2 tbsp warm water for soaking the mushrooms
10 large slices mild, lean prosciutto

For cooking the pasta
6 1/3 qt water
2 tbsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Put the dried mushrooms in the warm water and soak for 30 minutes. Drain, squeeze gently, and chop into small pieces.

2. Simmer the 4 gizzards in lightly salted water for 30 minutes. Drain and cut into small pieces.

3. Melt 1 1/2 tablespoons butter in a skillet. Add the gizzards, livers, and hearts and brown for 5 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

4. Make the meatballs. Combine the ground veal with the eggs, about 1/3 cup plus 1 tablespoon Parmigiano, and half of the fine salt.

5. Form very small meatballs about the size of olives.

6. Melt another 1 1/2 tablespoons butter in the same skillet and brown the meatballs in batches for 4–5 minutes, turning until colored on all sides.

7. Add the tomatoes, browned giblets, meatballs, and mushrooms. Add the remaining fine salt.

8. Cook over medium-low heat for 30 minutes, stirring gently, until a thick ragù forms. Turn off the heat.

9. Preheat the oven to 350°F.

10. Use about 2 teaspoons of the remaining butter to grease a deep baking dish or timballo mold thoroughly.

11. Line the bottom and sides with prosciutto, allowing the slices to hang over the rim so they can fold over the filling. Reserve enough prosciutto to cover any open areas on top.

12. Bring the pasta water and salt to a boil. Cook the fettuccine very al dente, about 2 minutes less than its normal cooking time.

13. Drain and toss the fettuccine with about two-thirds of the ragù and about 1/3 cup plus 1 tablespoon Parmigiano.

14. Fill the prosciutto-lined mold with the pasta. Spread the remaining ragù and about 3 tablespoons Parmigiano over the top.

15. Fold the overhanging prosciutto over the pasta and use the reserved slices to close the casing completely.

16. Dot the surface with the remaining butter.

17. Bake at 350°F for about 30 minutes, until the prosciutto is browned but not dried out.

18. Rest for 10 minutes.

19. Invert the timballo onto a warm serving platter and carefully remove the mold.

Service

Cut into 6 slices and serve hot.

Chef's note

Resting the baked timballo before inversion allows the pasta, ragù, meatballs, mushrooms, and prosciutto casing to settle so the finished timballo holds together cleanly when sliced.
history: A specialty of Anagni in Ciociaria, this elaborate timballo is associated with the historic Ristorante del Gallo and is dedicated to Pope Boniface VIII. Modern accounts place its creation in the 19th century; the protected house recipe remains closely guarded.
description: Firm egg fettuccine, rich ragù, tiny meatballs, giblets, mushrooms, and Parmigiano are baked inside a savory casing of prosciutto. Sliced at the table, it is theatrical, intensely meaty, and designed as a grand celebration dish.

title: Tonnarelli Cacio e Pepe
instructions:
Tonnarelli Cacio e Pepe

Roman tonnarelli with Pecorino Romano, toasted black pepper, and starch-rich pasta water.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

7/8 lb fresh tonnarelli
2 cups medium-aged Pecorino Romano, finely grated
3 tbsp whole black peppercorns
1 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
2 1/3 tsp fine salt
2 1/8 qt water
1 cup reserved pasta cooking water

Preparation

1. Finely grate the Pecorino Romano and divide it into two 1-cup portions.

2. Coarsely crush the black peppercorns.

3. Bring 2 1/8 quarts water and 2 1/3 teaspoons salt to a boil.

4. Cook the tonnarelli. After 3 minutes, remove 1 cup pasta water and keep it hot.

5. Heat a wide skillet over medium heat. Add the pepper and toast for 60 seconds.

6. Add the olive oil and 1/4 cup of the reserved pasta water. Cook for 1 minute.

7. Drain the tonnarelli 2 minutes before fully cooked and transfer it to the skillet.

8. Add another 1/4 cup pasta water and finish cooking for 2 minutes, moving the pasta continuously with tongs.

9. Put 1 cup Pecorino in a bowl. Gradually whisk in 1/4 cup hot pasta water until smooth.

10. Add another 1/2 cup Pecorino and 2 tablespoons pasta water. Whisk until thick but fluid.

11. Turn off the heat completely under the skillet.

12. Pour the Pecorino cream over the tonnarelli and toss vigorously with tongs for 60–90 seconds.

13. Add the final 1/2 cup Pecorino and remaining 2 tablespoons pasta water. Toss until glossy and uniform.

Serving

Divide among 4 plates and serve immediately.

Chef's Note

Add the Pecorino cream only after the heat is off. Residual heat and starch-rich pasta water emulsify the cheese without making it separate or turn grainy.
history: A close cousin of Rome’s classic cacio e pepe, this version uses tonnarelli, a thick square-cut fresh pasta especially popular in Lazio. The dish belongs to the same pastoral tradition built around durable pecorino, black pepper, and pasta water. Its place at the table endures.
description: Roman tonnarelli with Pecorino Romano, toasted black pepper, and starch-rich pasta water.

title: Roman Pasta and Chickpeas
instructions:
Roman Pasta and Chickpeas

A Roman chickpea-and-pasta soup scented with rosemary and enriched with anchovies and tomato.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

1 1/2 cups dried chickpeas
1 1/2 cups cannolicchi or maltagliati pasta
1 garlic clove
4 oil-packed anchovy fillets
2 tbsp tomato sauce
1/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil
2 rosemary sprigs
1 1/3 tsp fine salt
1/2 tsp ground black pepper
6 1/3 cups warm water for soaking
8 1/2 cups fresh water for cooking the chickpeas

Preparation

1. Put the chickpeas in a bowl with the warm soaking water and soak for 12 hours.

2. Drain and rinse the chickpeas.

3. Transfer them to a pot with the fresh cooking water and rosemary.

4. Bring to a gentle boil and cook over low heat for 2 hours, until tender but still intact.

5. Remove the rosemary. Measure and reserve 3 cups of chickpea cooking water.

6. Heat 3 tablespoons olive oil in a skillet. Add the whole garlic clove and cook for 2 minutes.

7. Add the anchovy fillets and mash them with a fork until dissolved into the oil.

8. Remove the garlic. Add the tomato sauce and cook over high heat for 3 minutes.

9. Pour the mixture into the pot with the chickpeas.

10. Add 2 cups reserved chickpea cooking water and 1 teaspoon salt. Simmer for 10 minutes.

11. Bring to a boil and add the pasta.

12. Cook for about 8 minutes, stirring regularly. Add the remaining 1 cup reserved chickpea water during cooking.

13. Turn off the heat and stir in the remaining 1 tablespoon olive oil, remaining 1/3 teaspoon salt, and black pepper.

14. Rest for 3 minutes.

Serving

Divide among 4 bowls and serve hot.

Chef's Note

The anchovies should dissolve completely into the oil, adding savory depth without leaving an overt fish flavor. The final rest allows the pasta starch to thicken the soup naturally.
history: Roman pasta and chickpeas has been documented for well over a century. The Roman hallmark is the addition of anchovy to the chickpea base, along with rosemary, creating a deeply savory variation on Italy’s widespread tradition of combining pasta and legumes.
description: Tender chickpeas and small pasta simmer together in a rosemary-scented broth deepened with anchovy, garlic, and tomato. Creamy from natural starch rather than dairy, it is rustic, savory, warming, and substantial enough to stand alone as a meal.

title: Roman Pasta and Broccoli
instructions:
Roman Pasta and Broccoli

A Roman soup of broken spaghetti and Romanesco broccoli with anchovy, aromatic vegetables, tomato, and chile.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

2/3 lb spaghetti, broken into short lengths
1 Romanesco broccoli, about 1 3/4 lb
4 1/4 cups vegetable broth
2 garlic cloves
2 anchovy fillets
1/2 carrot
1/2 celery stalk
1/2 onion
2 tsp tomato paste
1 small red chile
1/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil
3/4 tsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Keep the vegetable broth hot at a gentle simmer.

2. Clean the broccoli, remove the outer leaves, and divide the head into florets. Cut the tender stems into 3/4-inch pieces.

3. Finely chop the carrot, celery, and onion.

4. Heat the olive oil in a large pot.

5. Add the crushed garlic, anchovy fillets, and halved chile. Cook for 1 minute.

6. Add the carrot, celery, and onion and cook over medium heat for 5 minutes.

7. Dissolve the tomato paste in 1/4 cup hot broth and pour it into the pot.

8. Add the broccoli florets and stems and cook for 10 minutes, stirring every 2 minutes.

9. Add the remaining 4 cups broth, cover, and cook over low heat for 10 minutes.

10. Remove about 2 cups intact florets and set aside.

11. Blend the soup for 20–30 seconds with an immersion blender, keeping a slightly rustic texture.

12. Return the whole florets to the pot and bring back to a boil.

13. Add the salt and broken spaghetti.

14. Cook the pasta directly in the soup for the package cooking time, stirring often.

Serving

Divide among 4 bowls and serve very hot.

Chef's Note

Reserve some whole florets before blending to preserve textural contrast. Cooking the spaghetti directly in the soup releases starch into the broth and creates a naturally creamier consistency.
history: Pasta with Romanesco broccoli belongs to Rome’s long tradition of vegetable-and-pasta minestra dishes, where inexpensive seasonal produce is stretched into a complete meal. Anchovy, garlic, chile, and tomato reflect the assertive pantry flavors typical of Roman home cooking.
description: A Roman soup of broken spaghetti and Romanesco broccoli with anchovy, aromatic vegetables, tomato, and chile.

title: Roman Pasta and Lentils
instructions:
Roman Pasta and Lentils

A lentil-and-mixed-pasta soup with carrot, celery, garlic, tomato, and potato.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

1 1/2 cups Italian lentils
2 1/2 cups mixed pasta
1 medium carrot
1 celery stalk
1 garlic clove
3 tbsp tomato sauce
2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
2 cups plus 2 tbsp vegetable broth
1 small potato

Preparation

1. Rinse the lentils thoroughly under cold water.

2. Finely chop the carrot, celery, and garlic.

3. Heat the olive oil in a medium pot.

4. Add the carrot, celery, and garlic and cook over medium heat for 5 minutes, stirring regularly.

5. Add the vegetable broth, tomato sauce, and lentils.

6. Peel the potato, cut it into 4 pieces, and add it to the pot.

7. Bring to a gentle boil, partially cover, and cook for 30 minutes.

8. Remove the potato pieces, mash them with a fork, and return them to the pot.

9. Add the mixed pasta.

10. Cook for 8–10 minutes, stirring often and checking the larger pasta shapes during the final 2 minutes.

11. Turn off the heat and rest for 5 minutes.

Serving

Divide among 4 bowls and serve hot.

Chef's Note

Mashed potato thickens the soup without flour or cream. Mixed pasta contains shapes with different cooking times, so checking the larger pieces during the final minutes keeps everything properly al dente.
history: Pasta and lentils is part of central Italy’s cucina povera tradition, built from inexpensive legumes, pasta, and aromatic vegetables. Roman household versions vary widely, but the essential idea remains the same: a thick, nourishing one-pot soup made creamy by starch rather than dairy.
description: A lentil-and-mixed-pasta soup with carrot, celery, garlic, tomato, and potato.

title: Potato Gnocchi with Castrato Ragù
instructions:
Potato Gnocchi with Castrato Ragù

Homemade potato gnocchi with a slow-cooked castrato ragù of red wine, tomato, and herbs.

Ingredients

For the gnocchi
about 2 1/4 lb potatoes
2 cups type 00 flour
1 egg
1 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
1/2 tsp fine salt

For the castrato ragù
about 1 1/2 lb castrato stew meat
1 celery stalk
1 small carrot
1 white onion
1 garlic clove
3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
1 cup red wine
2 cups tomato sauce
1 bay leaf
2 sage leaves
1 rosemary sprig
1 whole clove
1 1/3 tsp fine salt
1/2 tsp ground black pepper

For cooking the gnocchi
5 1/4 qt water
2 tbsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Peel the potatoes and steam until completely tender, about 25–30 minutes.

2. Rice them while still hot and spread them on the work surface for 5 minutes.

3. Add the salt, egg, and olive oil.

4. Gradually incorporate the flour and knead briefly until soft and even.

5. Divide the dough into ropes about 3/4 inch thick, cut into 3/4-inch pieces, and ridge them on a gnocchi board.

6. For the sauce, finely chop the onion, celery, carrot, and garlic.

7. Heat the olive oil in a pot and cook the vegetables over low heat for 8 minutes.

8. Add the castrato and brown for 10 minutes, turning the pieces on all sides.

9. Add the red wine and cook for 5 minutes, until the sharp alcohol aroma has evaporated.

10. Add the tomato sauce, bay leaf, sage, rosemary, clove, salt, and pepper.

11. Cover with the lid slightly ajar and cook over low heat for 90 minutes, stirring every 15 minutes.

12. Bring the cooking water and salt to a boil.

13. Cook the gnocchi in 3–4 batches.

14. Lift them out with a slotted spoon as soon as they float and transfer directly to the sauce.

15. Stir gently over low heat for 1 minute.

Serving

Divide into 6 portions and serve immediately.

Chef's Note

Work the gnocchi dough only until the flour is incorporated; prolonged kneading develops gluten and makes the gnocchi rubbery. Cook the ragù slowly until the castrato is very tender.

instructions:
Pappardelle with Hare Ragù

Pappardelle with hare marinated in red wine and slowly cooked with vegetables, tomato, sage, and bay leaf.

about 1 1/8 lb pappardelle

Preparation

1. Cut the hare into even pieces, rinse briefly, and dry thoroughly.

2. Place the meat in a bowl with the red wine, onion, garlic, carrot, celery, bay leaves, and sage.

3. Cover and refrigerate for at least 2 hours.

4. Drain the meat. Strain and reserve the wine. Cut the marinade vegetables into small pieces.

5. Heat the olive oil in a pot.

6. Brown the vegetables for 6 minutes.

7. Add the hare and brown on all sides for 10 minutes.

8. Add the strained wine and cook over low heat until completely evaporated, about 10 minutes.

9. Add the passata, salt, and pepper.

10. Cook over very low heat for 90 minutes with the lid slightly ajar.

11. Remove the hare pieces, strip the meat from the bones, and return it to the sauce.

12. Bring the pasta water and salt to a boil.

13. Cook the pappardelle al dente and drain.

14. Dress with the hare ragù and 6 tbsp pecorino.

Serving

The marinade seasons the game and builds the aromatic base of the ragù. Let the wine evaporate completely before adding tomato so the sauce does not retain a harsh wine flavor.

title: Pici with Aglione Tomato Sauce
instructions:
Pici with Aglione Tomato Sauce

Hand-rolled Tuscan pici with a sauce of Val di Chiana aglione garlic, tomato, and chile.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

For the pici
4 cups type 0 flour
1 cup plus 1 tbsp warm water
3/4 tsp fine salt
1 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
1/3 cup remilled durum semolina for dusting

For the sauce
5 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
4 large aglione garlic cloves or fresh garlic cloves
1 red chile
about 2 cups tomato pulp
3/4 tsp fine salt

For cooking the pici
5 1/4 qt water
2 tbsp coarse salt

Preparation

1. Put the flour in a large bowl and add the fine salt.

2. Add the olive oil and gradually pour in the warm water while mixing with a fork.

3. Transfer the dough to the work surface and knead for 10 minutes until smooth.

4. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.

5. For the sauce, heat the olive oil in a heavy-bottomed skillet.

6. Lightly crush the aglione cloves and add them with the chile.

7. Cook over low heat for 3 minutes without browning the garlic.

8. Add the tomato pulp and salt. Cook over low heat for 10 minutes.

9. Roll the dough to about 3/16 inch thick.

10. Cut into strips 3/8 inch wide and roll each strip on the work surface into a long picio.

11. Coat the pici lightly with semolina and arrange on a tray without overlapping.

12. Bring the cooking water and salt to a boil.

13. Cook the pici for about 5 minutes.

14. Drain al dente and transfer directly to the sauce.

15. Toss over medium heat for 1 minute.

Serving

Divide among 4 plates and serve immediately.

Chef's Note

Val di Chiana aglione has a sweeter, gentler flavor than ordinary garlic. Cooking it slowly without browning prevents bitterness and lets its aroma merge with the tomato.
history: Pici are a hand-rolled peasant pasta of southern Tuscany, especially Siena, Val d’Orcia, and Val di Chiana. Aglione is the large, mild garlic traditionally grown in Val di Chiana, making the tomato-and-garlic sauce one of the area’s defining pairings. Its place at the table endures.

instructions:
Gnudi with Butter and Sage

Tuscan ricotta-and-spinach gnudi, lightly floured and served with butter, sage, and Parmigiano Reggiano.

1 1/3 cups cooked spinach, drained and thoroughly squeezed

3 tbsp grated Parmigiano Reggiano

1/3 cup type 00 flour for coating

8 sage leaves
1/4 tsp freshly grated nutmeg
2/3 tsp fine salt

For cooking the gnudi
3 1/4 qt water
1 tbsp plus 1/2 tsp coarse salt

Preparation

1. Place the ricotta in a colander and refrigerate for at least 4 hours to drain.

2. Squeeze the spinach until no more water comes out, then finely chop it.

3. Combine the ricotta, spinach, 3 tablespoons Parmigiano, and egg in a bowl.

4. Add the nutmeg and fine salt. Mix with a fork until even.

5. Spread the flour on a tray.

6. Shape the mixture into 20 balls slightly smaller than a walnut and roll them gently in the flour.

7. Bring the cooking water and salt to a boil.

8. Meanwhile, melt the butter in a skillet and add the sage leaves.

9. Cook the butter and sage over medium-low heat for 3 minutes, until the butter smells nutty without turning dark.

10. Cook the gnudi in 2 batches. Lift them out with a slotted spoon as soon as they rise to the surface.

11. Transfer directly to the butter and sage and roll gently for 30 seconds.

Serving

Divide among 4 plates and finish with the remaining 3 tablespoons Parmigiano Reggiano.

Chef's Note

The ricotta and spinach must be very dry. Excess moisture makes the mixture fragile and forces the use of more flour, while thorough draining keeps the gnudi tender but stable during boiling.

instructions:
Tortelli Maremmani

Large Maremma-style tortelli filled with spinach and chard, sheep's-milk ricotta, eggs, Parmigiano, and nutmeg, finished with butter and sage.

Yield: 6 servings

Ingredients

For the pasta dough
4 cups type 0 or all-purpose flour

1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper

For finishing
4 tbsp butter
8 fresh sage leaves
2/3 cup finely grated Parmigiano Reggiano

For cooking the tortelli
6 1/3 qt water
2 tbsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Make the pasta dough. Mound the flour on the work surface. Beat the 4 eggs with the salt and pour them into the center.

2. Incorporate the flour with a fork, then knead by hand for 10–12 minutes, until smooth, elastic, and fairly firm.

3. Wrap the dough and rest for 30 minutes.

4. Wash the spinach and chard thoroughly. Put them in a pot while still wet from the final rinse, cover, and cook over medium heat for 5–7 minutes, until wilted.

5. Drain, cool, and squeeze the greens very dry. Chop finely with a knife.

6. Mix the greens, ricotta, 2 eggs, 4 tablespoons Parmigiano, nutmeg, salt, and pepper until uniform.

7. Roll the pasta thin, about 1/32 inch, and cut into even strips.

8. Place a heaping teaspoon of filling every 3 inches along one half of each strip.

9. Fold the pasta over the filling. Press around each mound to expel air and seal completely.

10. Cut the tortelli with a fluted wheel, leaving a broad border of pasta around the filling.

11. Arrange on a semolina-dusted tray and dry for 20 minutes.

12. Bring the cooking water and salt to a boil. Cook the tortelli in batches for at least 10 minutes, then lift them out gently with a slotted spoon.

13. Melt the butter in a wide skillet over low heat. Add the sage and cook for 2 minutes without browning the butter.

14. Layer the tortelli on a warm serving platter, seasoning each layer with sage butter and Parmigiano.

15. Rest for 2 minutes before serving.

Service

Divide into 6 portions and serve hot.

Chef's note

The filling should be dry and the pasta thin but strong. The characteristic broad pasta border helps keep the filling sealed during the relatively long cooking time.

11. Bring the cooking water and salt to a boil.

12. Cook the tortelli in batches for 3–4 minutes, until the pasta is cooked and the filling is hot.

14. Dress the tortelli with the sage butter and scatter the Parmigiano over them.

title: Testaroli with Pesto
instructions:
Testaroli with Pesto

Lunigiana-style testaroli cooked as thin skillet cakes, cut into diamonds, briefly boiled, and dressed with pesto.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

3 1/3 cups type 00 flour
2 1/2 cups water
1/3 tsp fine salt
1/2 cup plus 1 tbsp pesto
1 tbsp olive oil for greasing the pan

For cooking the testaroli
3 1/4 qt water
1 tbsp fine salt

Preparation

1. Put the flour and salt in a large bowl.

2. Gradually add the water while whisking continuously until the batter is completely smooth and free of lumps.

3. Rest the batter for 15 minutes.

4. Heat an 8-inch nonstick skillet over medium heat.

5. Grease the surface very lightly with some of the olive oil.

6. Pour in about two ladles of batter and rotate the skillet to form an even disk about 1/8 inch thick.

7. Cook for 3–4 minutes, until the underside is set and lightly colored.

8. Turn and cook the second side for 1 minute.

9. Transfer to a cutting board and cool. Repeat with the remaining batter.

10. Cut the disks into strips about 2 inches wide and then into diamond shapes.

11. Bring the cooking water and salt to a boil.

12. Add the testaroli and cook for 3 minutes.

13. Drain gently and transfer to a large bowl.

14. Add the pesto and fold gently until every piece is evenly coated.

Service

Divide among 4 plates and serve hot.

Chef's note

instructions:
Pappardelle with Wild Boar Ragù

Tuscan pappardelle with red-wine-marinated wild boar, pork, beef, tomato, and aromatic herbs.

Yield: 4–6 servings

1 1/8 lb egg pappardelle

Preparation

1. Put the wild boar in a nonreactive bowl with 1 2/3 cups red wine, the carrot, celery, onion, half of the parsley, bay leaves, rosemary, juniper, and whole cloves.

2. Cover and marinate in the refrigerator overnight.

3. Drain the wild boar and vegetables. Discard the marinade liquid.

4. Heat the olive oil in a wide pot. Add the marinated vegetables and garlic and cook for 8 minutes.

5. Add the wild boar and brown for 6 minutes.

6. Add the beef and pork and continue browning for another 6 minutes.

7. Pour in the remaining 1/3 cup plus 1 tablespoon red wine and cook for 3 minutes.

8. Add the passata, salt, and pepper.

9. Cover with the lid slightly ajar and cook over low heat for at least 2 hours, stirring every 20 minutes.

10. Remove the lid and cook for another 30 minutes, until the ragù is thick but still fluid.

11. Remove the bay leaves, rosemary, and whole cloves. Add the remaining parsley.

12. Bring the pasta water and salt to a boil. Cook the pappardelle until al dente.

13. Drain and immediately dress with the wild-boar ragù.

Service

Divide into 4–6 portions and serve very hot.

Chef's note

The overnight marinade softens the wild character of the meat. Use fresh wine for the final deglazing rather than the marinade liquid.

instructions:
Cuttlefish-ink Risotto

Carnaroli risotto with cuttlefish, cuttlefish ink, dry white wine, vegetable broth, Parmigiano, and parsley.

Yield: 4 servings

Ingredients

1 3/4 cups Carnaroli rice
7/8 lb cleaned cuttlefish

1/3 cup plus 1 tbsp finely grated Parmigiano Reggiano
1/2 cup finely chopped fresh parsley

Preparation

1. Keep the vegetable broth at a gentle simmer.

2. Cut part of the cuttlefish into 3/8-inch cubes and the remainder into thin strips. Separate the tentacles.

3. Heat 2 tablespoons olive oil in a high-sided saucepan. Add the shallot and cook over medium-low heat for 4 minutes.

4. Add the cuttlefish and cook for 2 minutes.

5. Add the rice and toast for 2 minutes, stirring continuously.

6. Pour in the white wine and cook until almost completely absorbed, about 2–3 minutes.

7. Add one ladle of hot broth and stir. Continue adding broth one ladle at a time as each addition is nearly absorbed.

8. After about 8 minutes, dissolve the cuttlefish ink in 1/4 cup hot broth and add it to the rice.

9. Continue cooking for another 8–10 minutes, until the rice is al dente and creamy.

10. Turn off the heat. Add the Parmigiano, remaining 1 tablespoon olive oil, parsley, salt, and pepper.

11. Stir vigorously for 1 minute.

12. Cover and rest for 2 minutes.

Service

Divide among 4 warm plates and serve immediately.

Chef's note

Adding the ink halfway through cooking distributes it evenly while preserving its intensity. Finish the risotto off the heat so it remains loose and glossy.

title: Polenta Incatenata
instructions:
Polenta Incatenata

Lunigiana-style soft polenta with cranberry beans, Tuscan kale, potatoes, carrots, onion, garlic, and grated cheese.

Yield: 6–8 servings

Ingredients

1 cup dried cranberry beans
1 large bunch lacinato kale
2 large potatoes
2 carrots
1 medium yellow onion
2 garlic cloves

2 tsp fine salt, divided
10 1/2 cups water for the vegetables and polenta

For soaking and precooking the beans
6 1/3 cups water for soaking
6 1/3 cups fresh water for precooking

Preparation

1. Rinse the beans. Put them in a bowl with the soaking water and baking soda and soak overnight.

2. Drain and rinse the beans.

3. Put them in a pot with the fresh water and 2/3 teaspoon salt. Bring to a boil and simmer for 20 minutes, until almost tender. Drain.

4. Remove the tough ribs from the kale and slice the leaves into ribbons.

5. Peel the potatoes and cut into 3/4-inch cubes. Slice the carrots. Chop the onion and garlic.

6. Put the beans, kale, potatoes, carrots, onion, and garlic in a heavy pot with the 10 1/2 cups water and 1/2 cup olive oil.

7. Bring to a boil, skim any foam, and add the remaining salt.

8. Simmer over medium-low heat for 30 minutes.

9. Slowly stream in the cornmeal while stirring continuously with a whisk or sturdy wooden spoon.

10. Cook for 35–45 minutes, stirring often and scraping the bottom and sides, until thick but still pourable.

11. Adjust the consistency with a small amount of hot water only if the polenta becomes too stiff.

Service

Ladle into 6–8 bowls. Finish with the grated cheese and the reserved 2 tablespoons olive oil.

Chef's note

Add the cornmeal slowly to prevent lumps. The finished dish should remain softer than sliceable polenta, with the beans and vegetables distributed throughout.

Matuffi

Soft Versilia-style polenta layered with hot meat ragù and Parmigiano.

1. Bring the water to a boil in a heavy-bottomed pot.

3. Slowly stream in the cornmeal while whisking continuously.

4. Once all of the cornmeal is incorporated, switch to a wooden spoon.

5. Cook over low heat for about 30 minutes, stirring very frequently, until the polenta is very soft and smooth.

6. Keep the meat ragù hot.

7. Spoon about 3 tablespoons ragù into the bottom of each shallow bowl.

8. Cover with a layer of soft polenta.

9. Repeat the ragù and polenta layers until the bowl is filled, making at least three layers total.

10. Finish with a small amount of ragù.

Divide the Parmigiano among the four bowls and serve immediately.

Chef's note

Matuffi should remain soft enough to layer. The polenta is not meant to hold its own shape; it should merge with the ragù in each spoonful.

Gnocchi with Goose Ragù

Umbrian potato gnocchi with slow goose ragù, white wine, tomato, rosemary, sage, and bay.

4. Add the garlic, rosemary, sage, and bay and cook for another 2 minutes.

5. Return the goose to the pot. Pour in the wine and cook for 3–4 minutes.

6. Add the tomatoes, salt, and pepper.

7. Cover with the lid slightly ajar and cook over very low heat for 60–75 minutes.

8. Remove the rosemary, sage, and bay. Coarsely shred the goose into the sauce.

9. For the gnocchi, boil the whole unpeeled potatoes for 25–30 minutes. Peel while hot and pass through a ricer.

10. Cool for 5 minutes. Add the salt, nutmeg, egg, and flour.

11. Knead only until the dough comes together.

12. Roll into ropes, cut into 3/4-inch pieces, and ridge on a gnocchi board or fork.

13. Bring the cooking water and salt to a boil.

14. Cook the gnocchi in small batches. Lift them out as soon as they float and transfer directly to the ragù.

15. Fold together gently.

Service

Divide among 4 plates and finish with the Umbrian Pecorino.

Chef's note

Work the gnocchi dough as little as possible. Simmer the goose ragù slowly until the meat shreds easily.

instructions:
Macco with Cannellini Beans

Umbrian polenta with cannellini beans, ham-bone broth, tomato, onion, celery, battuto, and Pecorino.

Yield: 6 servings

Ingredients

2 1/4 cups cornmeal

For soaking and cooking the beans
